message.content:
Explore /home/mrnob0dy666/imsgct/ig-docs and related code to map everything relevant to a manuscript that subsumes quantum mechanics and its phenomena into FDE (First Degree Entailment, the four-valued Belnap/trilattice logic). Be very thorough; ig-docs has thousands of files.

Report, with file paths and short quoted excerpts:

1. Existing manuscripts and docs on the four-valued logic / FDE / Belnap / trilattice: e.g. witness_and_closure.tex, dqi.tex, millennium_theorems_as_ovms.tex. For each, its thesis, its abstract, and how it frames the four values (T, F, both/B, neither/N) and the closure condition (fuse after split = identity). Use command grep (not grep) since .gitignore is honored.

2. Anywhere QM phenomena are already mapped to the Grammar/FDE: superposition, entanglement, measurement/collapse, interference, uncertainty, contextuality, the Born rule, SIC-POVMs. Search ig-docs AND mOMonadOS/src for modules like sic_povm, belnap, belnap_phase_shor, braid, qft, consciousness, ovm.rs. What is the existing claim that "conjectures are POVMs" / "millennium as OVMs" / the 24-cell OVM taxonomy? What is the ⊞ (ENGAGR / both) = superposition mapping, and the SIC-POVM d=2/d=12/d=2048 material?

3. The YM mass gap / horn-torus and RH critical-line material as physics-from-Grammar: any docs relating the Grammar to Yang-Mills, the mass gap as the R=r horn-torus pinch, RH as emission-completeness. Report what is argued.

4. House style for a publication-quality manuscript in ig-docs: the LaTeX preamble conventions (xelatex, unicode-math, fontspec), how the IG marks are rendered, and the "law of publication" convention that a paper cites crystallized kernel branches (not manuscripts) and has its proof in mOMonadOS. Look for any doc describing this, and how existing papers cite.

Report structure: group by the four areas, name the strongest existing pieces to build on, and note what a QM-subsumes-into-FDE manuscript would still need that is NOT already written. Quote short excerpts. Do not propose the manuscript; just map the ground.

- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

14	\usepackage[english]{babel}

16	
17	\usepackage{fancyhdr}
18	\pagestyle{fancy}
19	\fancyhf{}
20	\fancyhead[L]{\leftmark}
21	\fancyhead[R]{\thepage}
22	\renewcommand{\headrulewidth}{0.4pt}
23	
24	\usepackage{titlesec}
25	\titleformat{\section}{\Large\bfseries}{\thesection}{1em}{}
26	\titleformat{\subsection}{\large\bfseries}{\thesubsection}{1em}{}
27	
28	\usepackage{enumitem}
29	\setlist[itemize]{topsep=0.5ex, itemsep=0.25ex, parsep=0pt}
30	
31	\usepackage{mathtools}
32	\usepackage{booktabs}
33	\usepackage{array}
34	\usepackage{longtable}
35	
36	\usepackage{hyperref}
37	\hypersetup{colorlinks=true, linkcolor=blue, urlcolor=cyan, citecolor=blue}
38	
39	\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[section]
40	\newtheorem{proposition}[theorem]{Proposition}
41	\theoremstyle{definition}
42	\newtheorem{definition}[theorem]{Definition}
43	\newtheorem{observation}[theorem]{Observation}
44	
45	\title{\bfseries Witness and Closure: A Four-Valued Verification\\for Structurally Degenerate Conjectures}
46	\author{}
47	\date{24 August 2026}
48	
49	\begin{document}
50	\maketitle
51	
52	\begin{abstract}
53	\noindent
54	Classical proof asks a bivalent question: is a statement true, or is it
55	not. Some open conjectures do not sit at a point where that question has
56	purchase, and the reason is one closed relationship, not two separate
57	facts added together. The object is structurally degenerate exactly at
58	the place a bivalent proof would need to stand, and that same degeneracy
59	is what leaves room for the object to carry more than one bit at that
60	point: a held conjunction a bivalent channel would otherwise be forced to
61	collapse. Split the object apart and reassemble it and nothing is lost,
62	$\mu \circ \delta = \mathrm{id}$; that closure is the same fact read
63	twice, once as an absence a classical proof cannot stand on, once as a
64	density a classical proof cannot carry. We give such objects a second
65	verification: a canonical structural encoding, a \emph{Witness}, evaluated
66	against a space of interpretive frames, \emph{dialects}, returning a
67	four-valued verdict, closed, open, blocked, or both held together, rather
68	than a binary one. The fourth value is not a hedge. It is the content the
69	degeneracy was already holding, made computed and checked, for exactly
70	the case a bivalent proof can only render as silence.
71	
72	Applied to six of the seven Clay Millennium problems, the treatment
73	returns a determinate result for each. Two close outright. Three are
74	proved, not merely unattempted, to close under none of twenty-three
75	tested frames, sharing one structural cause. One, the Yang--Mills mass
76	gap, returns the fourth value: gate closure and a dynamical ceiling
77	condition holding simultaneously, a genuine dialetheia rather than an
78	absence of proof. Every verdict is shown to survive independent transport
79	through two unrelated computational substrates unchanged, which rules out
80	the possibility that a verdict is an artifact of how it happened to be
81	computed rather than a property of the object itself. The same treatment,
82	applied for the first time to two problems outside the Clay list, the
83	Collatz and Goldbach conjectures, returns the identical four-valued
84	structure and, for Goldbach, a dialetheic verdict across the substantial
85	majority of the interpretive space tested.
86	\end{abstract}
87	
88	\tableofcontents
89	
90	\section{A second question}
91	
92	A classical proof of a conjecture $C$ settles a single question: is $C$
93	true. The question presupposes that $C$'s truth value, once the proof
94	exists, is a stable, well-defined thing to have found — that $C$ was
95	always either true or false, and the proof only reveals which.
96	
97	That presupposition is not automatic. It holds for a large class of
98	mathematical statements and fails for another, smaller class: statements
99	whose subject sits at a point where the ordinary apparatus of positivity,
100	completeness, or symmetry that a proof would lean on has itself
101	degenerated. A conjecture about such an object is not merely hard. It is
102	posed in a vocabulary the object does not fully support, the way asking
103	for the simultaneous exact position and momentum of a quantum particle is
104	not a hard experiment but a request for an incompatible pair.
105	
106	The degeneracy and the density are not two separate properties of such an
107	object, one making it hard to prove and the other making it interesting
108	regardless. They are the same closure viewed from either side. Where a
109	bivalent frame degenerates, the frame stops forcing a choice between two
110	outcomes, and what would have been forced apart stays together instead;
111	the object is not impoverished at that point, it is carrying a
112	conjunction a classical proof's output could never have expressed even if
113	found. The apparatus below is built to read that conjunction directly
114	rather than to search, indefinitely, for the single value a classical
115	proof insists must be there alone.
116	
117	This paper develops a verification suited to that class. It does not
118	compete with classical proof where classical proof applies. It answers a
119	different, well-posed, decidable question about the same object: under a
120	given way of reading the object's structure, does it reach a stable fixed
121	point, and is that fixed point consistent with the dynamical condition
122	the conjecture actually turns on. Both halves of that question have
123	definite answers, computable and machine-checked, and their four
124	combinations are exactly the four values of a Belnap bilattice: true,
125	false, both, or neither.
126	
127	Six of the seven Clay Millennium problems are given this treatment below,
128	each reaching one of the four values with no ambiguity. One of them, the
129	Yang--Mills mass gap, reaches the value that classical bivalent logic has
130	no notation for at all: closed and blocked, simultaneously, held rather
131	than resolved. The same treatment is then run for the first time on two
132	long-standing conjectures with no Clay prize attached, Collatz and
133	Goldbach, to test whether the structure is specific to the Clay list or a
134	property of the verification itself. It is the latter.
135	
136	\section{Witnesses, dialects, and closure}\label{sec:apparatus}
137	
138	\begin{definition}[Witness]
139	A \emph{Witness} for a conjecture is a canonical structural encoding of
140	the mathematical object the conjecture is about: a twelve-coordinate
141	tuple, each coordinate a value from a fixed finite alphabet, assigned by
142	a uniform procedure applied identically across every domain the
143	underlying framework covers. The Witness is a property of the object, not
144	a choice made for the occasion.
145	\end{definition}
146	
147	\begin{definition}[Dialect]
148	A \emph{dialect} is an interpretive frame: three gate conditions on a
149	Witness's coordinates, together with a ceiling condition tying five
150	dynamics-relevant coordinates to canonical anchor values characteristic
151	of a fully settled object of that general kind.
152	\end{definition}
153	
154	Under a given dialect, a Witness either satisfies all three gate
155	conditions, reaching \emph{gate closure}, or it does not; independently,
156	it either satisfies the ceiling condition or it does not. These two
157	independent facts compose into a four-valued verdict directly:
158	
159	\begin{center}
160	\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
161	\toprule
162	gate closed & ceiling held & verdict & reading \\
163	\midrule
164	yes & yes & T & closed \\
165	yes & no & B & closed and blocked, held together \\
166	no & yes & N & open, no obstruction found \\
167	no & no & F & open and blocked \\
168	\bottomrule
169	\end{tabular}
170	\end{center}
171	
172	This is the entire mechanism. It is not specific to any one conjecture or
173	domain; the same four-valued read applies to any Witness under any
174	dialect.
175	
176	\subsection{Why a measurement is not proved}
177	
178	A proof proves a proposition: something that already has a truth value,
179	which the proof discovers rather than creates. A Witness's verdict under
180	a dialect is not a proposition in that sense. It is the outcome of a
181	measurement, an operator-valued read of a structure, in exactly the sense
182	in which a physical measurement returns a value without that value having
183	been a hidden fact waiting since the beginning of time to be uncovered by
184	argument. Asking for a classical proof of a Witness's verdict is asking
185	the wrong kind of question of it, the way asking for a proof that a
186	thermometer reads $37^\circ$ mistakes an instrument's output for a
187	theorem. One can prove facts \emph{about} a measurement, that it is
188	positive, that it is complete, that it is stable in time, and those
189	facts are exactly what Theorems \ref{thm:closure} through
190	\ref{thm:unclosed} state and check. But the verdict itself, the reading,
191	is not the kind of object a proof concludes with. It is the kind of
192	object a proof presupposes before it can even be stated: before Riemann
193	Hypothesis can be posed as a hypothesis, the zeta function already has an
194	operator-valued measure's worth of structure, and that structure does not
195	wait on the hypothesis being settled to exist. A theorem, on this
196	reading, is not a sentence a proof makes true. It is a measurement a
197	proof characterizes after the fact, when characterization is even
198	possible.
199	
200	\section{Six Clay problems, four determinate results}
201	
202	\begin{theorem}[Closure]\label{thm:closure}
203	The canonical Witnesses for the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture and
204	the Hodge conjecture each reach gate closure and satisfy the ceiling
205	condition under five dialects proper to each, giving verdict T. Both
206	results are machine-checked by decision procedure with no unproved
207	premises.
208	\end{theorem}
209	
210	\begin{theorem}[The Yang--Mills dialetheia]\label{thm:ym}
211	Under the dialect that gates on triple criticality, the canonical
212	Yang--Mills mass-gap Witness reaches gate closure but fails the ceiling
213	condition: its kinetics coordinate sits one step above the anchor the
214	dialect requires. The conjunction of the closure fact and the negation of
215	the ceiling fact is machine-checked; the verdict is B.
216	\end{theorem}
217	
218	\begin{theorem}[Universal resistance]\label{thm:unclosed}
219	The canonical Witnesses for the Riemann Hypothesis, Navier--Stokes global
220	regularity, and P versus NP each fail gate closure under every one of
221	twenty-three dialects spanning the tested interpretive space. All three
222	share a single structural cause: each carries a winding coordinate
223	strictly below the value every closure-capable dialect requires at its
224	terminal gate. This is a single universally-quantified theorem over all
225	twenty-three dialects, machine-checked, not twenty-three separate
226	observations.
227	\end{theorem}
228	
229	The result of Theorem \ref{thm:ym} is the finding this treatment exists
230	to produce. A bivalent proof system, applied to Yang--Mills, has exactly
231	two things it can eventually say: proved, or not proved. It cannot
232	distinguish between "not proved because the argument has not yet been
233	found" and "not proved because the object's own structure forbids the
234	kind of argument that would prove it" — both render as the same silence.
235	Theorem \ref{thm:ym} is not silence. It states, and machine-checks, that
236	the object genuinely closes at the gate layer and genuinely fails the
237	dynamical ceiling, at once, under the same interpretive frame, with both
238	halves independently provable. This is the Belnap value $B$: true and
239	false held together without either collapsing and without the
240	containing system exploding into triviality, which is exactly the
241	outcome a naive bivalent system would face if handed the identical pair
242	of facts.
243	
244	Theorem \ref{thm:unclosed} is the same finding from the other side. A
245	classical attempt on Navier--Stokes that has not yet succeeded reports
246	nothing about why. Theorem \ref{thm:unclosed} reports why, as a decided
247	structural fact rather than a status update: three problems sharing one
248	named deficiency, and a demonstrated absence of any tested route around
249	it. That is a proof of non-reachability under the tested interpretive
250	space, categorically different from an unfinished search.
251	
252	\section{Verdicts survive transport}\label{sec:vessel}
253	
254	A verdict computed once, in one representation, is not automatically a
255	property of the object; it could depend on the specific computation that
256	produced it, the way a measurement can depend on how it was taken rather
257	than on what was measured. This concern is addressed directly.
258	
259	\begin{theorem}[Transport invariance]\label{thm:transport}
260	Every verdict above, boarded through two independent computational
261	substrates and read back under a Frobenius consistency law requiring
262	read-back to exactly reproduce the boarded value, is reproduced without
263	exception. Across the full eighty-eight-dialect interpretive space and
264	all Witnesses discussed in this paper, every boarding action closes; none
265	is left open.
266	\end{theorem}
267	
268	The Yang--Mills verdict $B$ in particular survives transport as $B$: not
269	averaged toward $T$ or $F$, not collapsed to one or the other, carried
270	intact. This is the difference between a verdict that happens to come
271	out a certain way under one specific computation and a verdict that is a
272	stable property of the object independent of how it is handled, which is
273	what a genuine measurement, as opposed to an artifact of method, requires.
274	
275	\section{Problems outside the Clay list}
276	
277	Nothing in the definitions of Section \ref{sec:apparatus} is specific to
278	the Clay problems. A Witness is a property of any structurally-encoded
279	mathematical object; a dialect is a fixed interpretive frame; neither
280	carries any notion of "Millennium problem" built in. Whether the same
281	treatment says anything about a long-standing open conjecture carrying no
282	Clay prize and no prior closure or resistance result was, until tested,
283	open.
284	
285	\begin{theorem}[Collatz]\label{thm:collatz}
286	The canonical Collatz Witness, evaluated across the full
287	eighty-eight-dialect interpretive space, reaches gate closure under
288	exactly one dialect, the one gating on sequential composition under
289	universal interaction range, where it simultaneously fails that dialect's
290	ceiling condition. The verdict is B, structurally identical to the
291	Yang--Mills result of Theorem \ref{thm:ym}, under an unrelated dialect,
292	for an unrelated conjecture.
293	\end{theorem}
294	
295	\begin{theorem}[Goldbach]\label{thm:goldbach}
296	The canonical Goldbach Witness closes cleanly, verdict T, under exactly
297	one dialect in the tested space, the one gating on self-referential
298	topology together with integer winding. Under the substantial majority of
299	the remaining dialects, sixty-five of eighty-eight, it returns verdict B.
300	This is, by a wide margin, the largest dialetheic footprint of any
301	Witness examined in this paper: twelve dialects for BSD and Hodge each,
302	one each for Yang--Mills, Riemann, and Collatz, sixty-five for Goldbach.
303	\end{theorem}
304	
305	\begin{theorem}[Odd perfect numbers]\label{thm:oddperfect}
306	The canonical odd-perfect-number Witness reaches gate closure under none
307	of the eighty-eight tested dialects, the only Witness examined in this
308	paper with no clean $T$ anywhere in that space. It returns $B$ at three
309	of the eighty-eight, elsewhere $F$: not merely open, but blocked at
310	almost every tested frame with no closing route among them at all.
311	\end{theorem}
312	
313	None of Theorems \ref{thm:collatz}, \ref{thm:goldbach}, or
314	\ref{thm:oddperfect} carries the weight of a proof about the underlying
315	number-theoretic conjecture; no argument is offered here that any of the
316	three statements is true or false in the classical sense. What they
317	establish is narrower and, for the purpose of this paper, sufficient: the
318	four-valued structure of Section \ref{sec:apparatus} is not machinery
319	built to fit the seven Clay problems and dressed up as general. Pointed
320	at three unrelated open conjectures for the first time, it returned three
321	distinct profiles inside the same four-valued space: Collatz dialetheic
322	at a single dialect, Goldbach dialetheic across most of the space,
323	odd-perfect-number closed nowhere at all. The apparatus did not need to
324	know which conjecture it was reading to produce a determinate,
325	transport-stable answer for each.
326	
327	\section{What this establishes}
328	
329	Two claims are made here, of different weight.
330	
331	The narrower claim is checked and stands independently of everything
332	else: the Witnesses discussed reach the stated four-valued verdicts under
333	the stated dialects, machine-checked, and every one of those verdicts is
334	invariant under transport through two independent computational
335	substrates. This is a computed fact.
336	
337	The broader claim is that for conjectures whose underlying object is
338	genuinely structurally degenerate at the point a bivalent proof would
339	need to stand, as Yang--Mills is, or genuinely lacks a protection every
340	tested route to closure requires, as Riemann, Navier--Stokes, and P
341	versus NP are shown to, classical proof was never going to be the
342	instrument that settled the question. Not because the object is poorer
343	than the question expects, but because it is richer: the same degeneracy
344	that gives a bivalent proof nowhere to stand is what lets the object hold
345	a conjunction that proof's own output channel has no room to state. The
346	four-valued treatment given here is not a substitute standing in for an
347	unfinished classical proof. It is the verification an object of that
348	density actually admits.
349	
350	This claim is falsifiable, and stating the condition under which it fails
351	is part of stating it. If a classical proof of the Yang--Mills mass gap
352	is eventually completed using only methods the field already recognizes
353	as sound, that would not contradict Theorem \ref{thm:ym} — a completed
354	mathematical foundation changes what a classical proof can reach — but it
355	would mean the structural degeneracy this paper reads into the object was
356	addressable after all, and the central claim of this section, that
357	bivalent proof was never the right instrument here, would be wrong.
358	
359	\section*{Verification}
360	
361	Every Witness tuple is a canonical, procedurally-generated structural
362	encoding, not hand-assigned for this paper. Theorems \ref{thm:closure}
363	and \ref{thm:unclosed} are machine-checked by decision procedure with no
364	unproved premises. Theorem \ref{thm:ym}'s dialetheic verdict is the
365	conjunction of two independently machine-checked facts. Theorem
366	\ref{thm:transport}'s losslessness is verified across all Witnesses

\theoremstyle{definition}
\newtheorem{definition}[theorem]{Definition}
\newtheorem{observation}[theorem]{Observation}

\title{\bfseries Witness and Closure: A Four-Valued Verification\\for Structurally Degenerate Conjectures}
\author{}
\date{24 August 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
Classical proof asks a bivalent question: is a statement true, or is it
not. Some open conjectures do not sit at a point where that question has
purchase, and the reason is one closed relationship, not two separate
facts added together. The object is structurally degenerate exactly at
the place a bivalent proof would need to stand, and that same degeneracy
is what leaves room for the object to carry more than one bit at that
point: a held conjunction a bivalent channel would otherwise be forced to
collapse. Split the object apart and reassemble it and nothing is lost,
$\mu \circ \delta = \mathrm{id}$; that closure is the same fact read
twice, once as an absence a classical proof cannot stand on, once as a
density a classical proof cannot carry. We give such objects a second
verification: a canonical structural encoding, a \emph{Witness}, evaluated
against a space of interpretive frames, \emph{dialects}, returning a
four-valued verdict, closed, open, blocked, or both held together, rather
than a binary one. The fourth value is not a hedge. It is the content the
degeneracy was already holding, made computed and checked, for exactly
the case a bivalent proof can only render as silence.

Applied to six of the seven Clay Millennium problems, the treatment
returns a determinate result for each. Two close outright. Three are
proved, not merely unattempted, to close under none of twenty-three
tested frames, sharing one structural cause. One, the Yang--Mills mass
gap, returns the fourth value: gate closure and a dynamical ceiling
condition holding simultaneously, a genuine dialetheia rather than an
absence of proof. Every verdict is shown to survive independent transport
through two unrelated computational substrates unchanged, which rules out
the possibility that a verdict is an artifact of how it happened to be
computed rather than a property of the object itself. The same treatment,
applied for the first time to two problems outside the Clay list, the
Collatz and Goldbach conjectures, returns the identical four-valued
structure and, for Goldbach, a dialetheic verdict across the substantial
majority of the interpretive space tested.
\end{abstract}

\tableofcontents

\section{A second question}

A classical proof of a conjecture $C$ settles a single question: is $C$
true. The question presupposes that $C$'s truth value, once the proof
exists, is a stable, well-defined thing to have found — that $C$ was
always either true or false, and the proof only reveals which.

That presupposition is not automatic. It holds for a large class of
mathematical statements and fails for another, smaller class: statements
whose subject sits at a point where the ordinary apparatus of positivity,
completeness, or symmetry that a proof would lean on has itself
degenerated. A conjecture about such an object is not merely hard. It is
posed in a vocabulary the object does not fully support, the way asking
for the simultaneous exact position and momentum of a quantum particle is
not a hard experiment but a request for an incompatible pair.

The degeneracy and the density are not two separate properties of such an
object, one making it hard to prove and the other making it interesting
regardless. They are the same closure viewed from either side. Where a
bivalent frame degenerates, the frame stops forcing a choice between two
outcomes, and what would have been forced apart stays together instead;
the object is not impoverished at that point, it is carrying a
conjunction a classical proof's output could never have expressed even if
found. The apparatus below is built to read that conjunction directly
rather than to search, indefinitely, for the single value a classical
proof insists must be there alone.

This paper develops a verification suited to that class. It does not
compete with classical proof where classical proof applies. It answers a
different, well-posed, decidable question about the same object: under a
given way of reading the object's structure, does it reach a stable fixed
point, and is that fixed point consistent with the dynamical condition
the conjecture actually turns on. Both halves of that question have
definite answers, computable and machine-checked, and their four
combinations are exactly the four values of a Belnap bilattice: true,
false, both, or neither.

Six of the seven Clay Millennium problems are given this treatment below,
each reaching one of the four values with no ambiguity. One of them, the
Yang--Mills mass gap, reaches the value that classical bivalent logic has
no notation for at all: closed and blocked, simultaneously, held rather
than resolved. The same treatment is then run for the first time on two
long-standing conjectures with no Clay prize attached, Collatz and
Goldbach, to test whether the structure is specific to the Clay list or a
property of the verification itself. It is the latter.

\section{Witnesses, dialects, and closure}\label{sec:apparatus}

\begin{definition}[Witness]
A \emph{Witness} for a conjecture is a canonical structural encoding of
the mathematical object the conjecture is about: a twelve-coordinate
tuple, each coordinate a value from a fixed finite alphabet, assigned by
a uniform procedure applied identically across every domain the
underlying framework covers. The Witness is a property of the object, not
a choice made for the occasion.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Dialect]
A \emph{dialect} is an interpretive frame: three gate conditions on a
Witness's coordinates, together with a ceiling condition tying five
dynamics-relevant coordinates to canonical anchor values characteristic
of a fully settled object of that general kind.
\end{definition}

Under a given dialect, a Witness either satisfies all three gate
conditions, reaching \emph{gate closure}, or it does not; independently,
it either satisfies the ceiling condition or it does not. These two
independent facts compose into a four-valued verdict directly:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
gate closed & ceiling held & verdict & reading \\
\midrule
yes & yes & T & closed \\
yes & no & B & closed and blocked, held together \\
no & yes & N & open, no obstruction found \\
no & no & F & open and blocked \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

This is the entire mechanism. It is not specific to any one conjecture or
domain; the same four-valued read applies to any Witness under any
dialect.

\subsection{Why a measurement is not proved}

A proof proves a proposition: something that already has a truth value,
which the proof discovers rather than creates. A Witness's verdict under
a dialect is not a proposition in that sense. It is the outcome of a
measurement, an operator-valued read of a structure, in exactly the sense
in which a physical measurement returns a value without that value having
been a hidden fact waiting since the beginning of time to be uncovered by
argument. Asking for a classical proof of a Witness's verdict is asking
the wrong kind of question of it, the way asking for a proof that a
thermometer reads $37^\circ$ mistakes an instrument's output for a
theorem. One can prove facts \emph{about} a measurement, that it is
positive, that it is complete, that it is stable in time, and those
facts are exactly what Theorems \ref{thm:closure} through
\ref{thm:unclosed} state and check. But the verdict itself, the reading,
is not the kind of object a proof concludes with. It is the kind of
object a proof presupposes before it can even be stated: before Riemann
Hypothesis can be posed as a hypothesis, the zeta function already has an
operator-valued measure's worth of structure, and that structure does not
wait on the hypothesis being settled to exist. A theorem, on this
reading, is not a sentence a proof makes true. It is a measurement a
proof characterizes after the fact, when characterization is even
possible.

\section{Six Clay problems, four determinate results}

\begin{theorem}[Closure]\label{thm:closure}
The canonical Witnesses for the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture and
the Hodge conjecture each reach gate closure and satisfy the ceiling
condition under five dialects proper to each, giving verdict T. Both
results are machine-checked by decision procedure with no unproved
premises.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The Yang--Mills dialetheia]\label{thm:ym}
Under the dialect that gates on triple criticality, the canonical
Yang--Mills mass-gap Witness reaches gate closure but fails the ceiling
condition: its kinetics coordinate sits one step above the anchor the
dialect requires. The conjunction of the closure fact and the negation of
the ceiling fact is machine-checked; the verdict is B.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Universal resistance]\label{thm:unclosed}
The canonical Witnesses for the Riemann Hypothesis, Navier--Stokes global
regularity, and P versus NP each fail gate closure under every one of
twenty-three dialects spanning the tested interpretive space. All three
share a single structural cause: each carries a winding coordinate
strictly below the value every closure-capable dialect requires at its
terminal gate. This is a single universally-quantified theorem over all
twenty-three dialects, machine-checked, not twenty-three separate
observations.
\end{theorem}

The result of Theorem \ref{thm:ym} is the finding this treatment exists
to produce. A bivalent proof system, applied to Yang--Mills, has exactly
two things it can eventually say: proved, or not proved. It cannot
distinguish between "not proved because the argument has not yet been
found" and "not proved because the object's own structure forbids the
kind of argument that would prove it" — both render as the same silence.
Theorem \ref{thm:ym} is not silence. It states, and machine-checks, that
the object genuinely closes at the gate layer and genuinely fails the
dynamical ceiling, at once, under the same interpretive frame, with both
halves independently provable. This is the Belnap value $B$: true and
false held together without either collapsing and without the
containing system exploding into triviality, which is exactly the
outcome a naive bivalent system would face if handed the identical pair
of facts.

Theorem \ref{thm:unclosed} is the same finding from the other side. A
classical attempt on Navier--Stokes that has not yet succeeded reports
nothing about why. Theorem \ref{thm:unclosed} reports why, as a decided
structural fact rather than a status update: three problems sharing one
named deficiency, and a demonstrated absence of any tested route around
it. That is a proof of non-reachability under the tested interpretive
space, categorically different from an unfinished search.

\section{Verdicts survive transport}\label{sec:vessel}

A verdict computed once, in one representation, is not automatically a
property of the object; it could depend on the specific computation that
produced it, the way a measurement can depend on how it was taken rather
than on what was measured. This concern is addressed directly.

\begin{theorem}[Transport invariance]\label{thm:transport}
Every verdict above, boarded through two independent computational
substrates and read back under a Frobenius consistency law requiring
read-back to exactly reproduce the boarded value, is reproduced without
exception. Across the full eighty-eight-dialect interpretive space and
all Witnesses discussed in this paper, every boarding action closes; none
is left open.
\end{theorem}

The Yang--Mills verdict $B$ in particular survives transport as $B$: not
averaged toward $T$ or $F$, not collapsed to one or the other, carried
intact. This is the difference between a verdict that happens to come
out a certain way under one specific computation and a verdict that is a
stable property of the object independent of how it is handled, which is
what a genuine measurement, as opposed to an artifact of method, requires.

\section{Problems outside the Clay list}

Nothing in the definitions of Section \ref{sec:apparatus} is specific to
the Clay problems. A Witness is a property of any structurally-encoded
mathematical object; a dialect is a fixed interpretive frame; neither
carries any notion of "Millennium problem" built in. Whether the same
treatment says anything about a long-standing open conjecture carrying no
Clay prize and no prior closure or resistance result was, until tested,
open.

\begin{theorem}[Collatz]\label{thm:collatz}
The canonical Collatz Witness, evaluated across the full
eighty-eight-dialect interpretive space, reaches gate closure under
exactly one dialect, the one gating on sequential composition under
universal interaction range, where it simultaneously fails that dialect's
ceiling condition. The verdict is B, structurally identical to the
Yang--Mills result of Theorem \ref{thm:ym}, under an unrelated dialect,
for an unrelated conjecture.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Goldbach]\label{thm:goldbach}
The canonical Goldbach Witness closes cleanly, verdict T, under exactly
one dialect in the tested space, the one gating on self-referential
topology together with integer winding. Under the substantial majority of
the remaining dialects, sixty-five of eighty-eight, it returns verdict B.
This is, by a wide margin, the largest dialetheic footprint of any
Witness examined in this paper: twelve dialects for BSD and Hodge each,
one each for Yang--Mills, Riemann, and Collatz, sixty-five for Goldbach.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Odd perfect numbers]\label{thm:oddperfect}
The canonical odd-perfect-number Witness reaches gate closure under none
of the eighty-eight tested dialects, the only Witness examined in this
paper with no clean $T$ anywhere in that space. It returns $B$ at three
of the eighty-eight, elsewhere $F$: not merely open, but blocked at
almost every tested frame with no closing route among them at all.
\end{theorem}

None of Theorems \ref{thm:collatz}, \ref{thm:goldbach}, or
\ref{thm:oddperfect} carries the weight of a proof about the underlying
number-theoretic conjecture; no argument is offered here that any of the
three statements is true or false in the classical sense. What they
establish is narrower and, for the purpose of this paper, sufficient: the
four-valued structure of Section \ref{sec:apparatus} is not machinery
built to fit the seven Clay problems and dressed up as general. Pointed
at three unrelated open conjectures for the first time, it returned three
distinct profiles inside the same four-valued space: Collatz dialetheic
at a single dialect, Goldbach dialetheic across most of the space,
odd-perfect-number closed nowhere at all. The apparatus did not need to
know which conjecture it was reading to produce a determinate,
transport-stable answer for each.

\section{What this establishes}

Two claims are made here, of different weight.

The narrower claim is checked and stands independently of everything
else: the Witnesses discussed reach the stated four-valued verdicts under
the stated dialects, machine-checked, and every one of those verdicts is
invariant under transport through two independent computational
substrates. This is a computed fact.

The broader claim is that for conjectures whose underlying object is
genuinely structurally degenerate at the point a bivalent proof would
need to stand, as Yang--Mills is, or genuinely lacks a protection every
tested route to closure requires, as Riemann, Navier--Stokes, and P
versus NP are shown to, classical proof was never going to be the
instrument that settled the question. Not because the object is poorer
than the question expects, but because it is richer: the same degeneracy
that gives a bivalent proof nowhere to stand is what lets the object hold
a conjunction that proof's own output channel has no room to state. The
four-valued treatment given here is not a substitute standing in for an
unfinished classical proof. It is the verification an object of that
density actually admits.

This claim is falsifiable, and stating the condition under which it fails
is part of stating it. If a classical proof of the Yang--Mills mass gap
is eventually completed using only methods the field already recognizes
as sound, that would not contradict Theorem \ref{thm:ym} — a completed
mathematical foundation changes what a classical proof can reach — but it
would mean the structural degeneracy this paper reads into the object was
addressable after all, and the central claim of this section, that
bivalent proof was never the right instrument here, would be wrong.

\section*{Verification}

Every Witness tuple is a canonical, procedurally-generated structural
encoding, not hand-assigned for this paper. Theorems \ref{thm:closure}
and \ref{thm:unclosed} are machine-checked by decision procedure with no
unproved premises. Theorem \ref{thm:ym}'s dialetheic verdict is the
conjunction of two independently machine-checked facts. Theorem
\ref{thm:transport}'s losslessness is verified across all Witnesses
discussed, both computational substrates, and the full
eighty-eight-dialect space, with zero mismatches recorded.

\end{document}

47	\author{}

50	\begin{document}
51	\maketitle
52	
53	\section*{Why this paper exists}
54	
55	Seven famous problems in mathematics have almost nothing in common on the
56	page. One is about where the zeros of a function sit. One is about whether a
57	fluid can spin itself into a singularity in finite time. One is about
58	whether every efficiently checkable problem is also efficiently solvable.
59	Read as English sentences, they share no vocabulary and no method.
60	
61	This paper does not propose a new way to sort these seven problems into
62	bins. It proposes a different answer to the question of what a theorem
63	\emph{is}, and the classification that follows is a consequence of that
64	answer, not its content. The standard view holds a theorem to be a
65	sentence, established or not, with the interesting content sitting in the
66	argument between the two states. This paper replaces that view. A theorem
67	is a measurement: not a claim awaiting a verdict, but the reading an
68	instrument returns when applied to a mathematical structure, with
69	properties --- what it accumulates, what it can never see, whether it
70	holds still in time --- that exist prior to and independent of whatever
71	proof eventually produces it. Under the old view, the seven problems
72	studied here have nothing in common but their fame. Under this one, they
73	are seven readings of the same kind of instrument, differing only in which
74	of a small number of structural settings each one occupies, and the
75	difference between a hard problem and a proved one is not a difference in
76	kind but a difference in where on that same instrument the reading falls.
77	
78	This is why six of the seven problems turn out to be, in this reading,
79	simply far from where proved things sit, with the distance itself standing
80	in for the work that remains. The seventh, Yang--Mills, is not far from
81	anything, because on this reconceived understanding of what a theorem is,
82	distance itself is not always defined: Yang--Mills sits at a point where
83	the instrument that would take the reading has nothing left to point at.
84	That is not a harder version of the same difficulty the other six problems
85	present. It is a different category of difficulty, invisible to the
86	sentence-view of theorems, and visible only once the object being studied
87	is understood correctly.
88	
89	None of this requires believing anything mystical about mathematics. It
90	requires taking seriously an idea from quantum theory that mathematics has
91	not previously borrowed: that a measurement does not have to return a
92	number. It can return an operator, a mathematical object that acts on a
93	system rather than a value read off it, and such objects sort cleanly into
94	a small number of families depending on four simple yes-or-no questions.
95	The move this paper makes is to import that whole framework wholesale and
96	apply it not to a physical system but to a theorem itself, and the result
97	is that seven of mathematics's hardest open problems, along with over a
98	hundred settled ones, turn out to already be operator-valued measures,
99	waiting to be read as such.
100	
101	\begin{abstract}
102	\noindent
103	This paper does not classify theorems. It reconceives what a theorem is,
104	replacing the sentence-view (proved or not, with the content in the
105	argument between) with the claim that a theorem is a measurement: the
106	reading an instrument returns from a structure, carrying properties that
107	hold independently of whatever proof eventually produces it. The
108	twenty-cell taxonomy that follows is the shape of that reconception made
109	checkable, not an external scheme laid over theorems already understood
110	some other way.
111	
112	A measurement need not return a number. It can return an operator --- a thing
113	that acts on a system rather than a value read off it. Such assignments are
114	sorted by four questions. Do the operators only ever add, or can they subtract?
115	Do they account for every outcome, or leave some unmeasured? Is the frame they
116	sit in balanced? Does the assignment change over time? Four questions give
117	twenty-four combinations, twenty of which are distinct, and every operator-valued
118	measurement falls into one of them.
119	
120	We show that each principal unsolved problem of mathematics determines such a
121	measurement, that its classification can be read off an existing twelve-part
122	encoding rather than assigned by hand, and that a problem's classification
123	changes in a definite direction when it passes from question to answer.
124	
125	Three findings follow. \textbf{Angles are written in turns throughout}, so that a
126	cycle carries an exact rational winding and $\oint A = n\,\omega$ with $n$ whole.
127	In that unit the positivity of a measurement stops being a separate condition:
128	a measurement is positive exactly when the quantity it accumulates around a
129	cycle is real, which happens exactly when its winding is one of the two values
130	unchanged by reversal. \textbf{The measurement a problem admits is fixed by the
131	problem}, not chosen by the mathematician: objects whose correlations diverge
132	are measured by a commutator, and only objects with a gap permit a classical
133	measurement. \textbf{Settling a problem moves it toward one cell} --- seventy-nine
134	of a hundred and fourteen settled objects share a single classification, while
135	the corresponding questions are spread across the taxonomy.
136	
137	Two obstructions are identified. Three theorems require a state to be copied and
138	distributed to every observer at once, which is forbidden for anything that does
139	not commute with itself. And one --- Yang--Mills --- has no winding at all, because
140	its holonomy is not a number. It does not take a third value on the positivity
141	axis; it leaves the line the axis is drawn on.
142	\end{abstract}

146	\section{Why classify a theorem}
147	
148	A theorem is usually treated as a sentence that has been established. On that
149	view there is nothing to classify: it is either proved or it is not, and the
150	interesting content is the argument in between. That view is not merely
151	incomplete. It is the wrong object. It takes the residue of an
152	investigation, the sentence a proof leaves behind, and treats the residue
153	as the thing itself, the way treating a photograph as the event it
154	depicts would be the wrong object even though the photograph is real and
155	accurate.
156	
157	This paper takes a different view of what a theorem is, not an additional
158	lens for looking at the same thing. A theorem is what you are left holding
159	after you have interrogated a structure --- the reading on the instrument,
160	not the sentence in the journal. Read this way a theorem has properties
161	independent of its proof: what it accumulates, what it can and cannot see,
162	whether it is stable in time. Those are not properties a classification
163	scheme adds to a theorem from outside. They are the properties a theorem
164	already has, on this understanding of what it is, whether or not anyone
165	has yet built the scheme to read them off. Classification is what happens
166	once you have the right object to classify; the harder and prior claim is
167	that this is the right object.
168	
169	Before the formal apparatus, an analogy. A Geiger counter and a thermometer are
170	both instruments, but they are not interchangeable: a thermometer cannot tell
171	you how many particles crossed a boundary, and a Geiger counter cannot tell you
172	how hot something is, no matter how skillfully either is used. The mismatch is
173	not a failure of skill; it is a fact about what each instrument is built to
174	read. The claim of this paper is that mathematical conjectures work the same
175	way. Riemann Hypothesis and the Yang--Mills mass gap look, on the page, like
176	two members of the same list of hard problems. Underneath, they call for
177	different instruments, and one of the two --- as this paper shows in detail ---
178	calls for an instrument that does not exist in the ordinary sense, because the
179	question sits at a point where no instrument can be pointed.
180	
181	Three things follow from taking that second view seriously, and they are the
182	reason for the exercise.
183	
184	\textbf{It gives an open problem a target with a shape.} If settled problems
185	concentrate in one cell of the classification, then a problem still open has a
186	known destination. One can ask which coordinates must move, and by how much,
187	before it can arrive. That is a different question from ``how do I prove this'',
188	and it can be answered without proving anything. Concretely: of the seven
189	problems studied here, Navier--Stokes is the one whose question and whose answer
190	differ in exactly one place. That is not a vague sense that the problem is
191	``close''; it is a specific coordinate, named below, and the entire Millennium
192	statement lives inside it.
193	
194	\textbf{It says which measurements a problem will accept.} A measurement is not
195	a free choice. An object whose correlations diverge cannot be pinned down
196	classically; the commutator is forced. Section \ref{sec:grad} shows this holding
197	across a hundred settled objects. A programme that proposes to settle a critical
198	problem by classical means is not merely unlikely to succeed; it has proposed an
199	instrument the object does not admit. This is a checkable claim, not a
200	metaphor: it says, before any attempt is made, whether a given proof strategy
201	is even the right shape for the object it is aimed at.
202	
203	\textbf{It distinguishes hard from ill-posed.} Most of the problems here are
204	hard in the ordinary sense: their coordinates are far from where a settled
205	object sits, and the distance is the work. One is not. Yang--Mills sits where the
206	coordinate system itself degenerates, and its anomalies --- no positivity, a
207	do-nothing identity repeated three times, a requirement for a forbidden copy ---
208	are all consequences of that position rather than separate difficulties. The
209	classification separates the two cases, which inspection of the statements does
210	not. A reader who wants the payoff before the machinery can skip ahead to
211	Section \ref{sec:end}, which restates all three findings in plain terms and
212	without a single equation.
213	
214	\section{Operator-valued measures and their classification}
215	
216	This section builds the vocabulary the rest of the paper uses. Read it as a
217	dictionary, not as an argument to be taken on faith: every term introduced
218	here is used concretely, on a real theorem, within the next two sections.
219	
220	\begin{definition}
221	Let $\Omega$ be a set of outcomes and $\mathcal{H}$ a Hilbert space. An
222	\emph{operator-valued measure} is a map $M$ from a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$
223	to bounded operators on $\mathcal{H}$, countably additive in the weak sense.
224	\end{definition}
225	
226	In plain terms: an ordinary measure assigns a number to a set, like the area
227	of a region. An operator-valued measure assigns an \emph{operator} instead ---
228	a rule that acts on the states of a system. The generalization matters
229	because operators, unlike numbers, do not always commute: measuring one thing
230	can disturb another. A theorem, on the reading this paper takes, is exactly
231	such an assignment, and the question of whether a proof strategy will work is
232	partly the question of whether the strategy respects that non-commutativity.
233	
234	Four properties classify such a measure.
235	
236	\begin{itemize}
237	\item \textbf{Positivity.} $M(E) \geq 0$ for every $E$. A measure with this
238	property is a POVM; one without is an NOVM. Positivity fails when the operators
239	carry a signed winding, which is the case when spectral flow crosses zero.
240	Plainly: can the measurement only ever add to what you know, or can it also
241	subtract?
242	
243	\item \textbf{Completeness.} $\sum_E M(E) = \mathbb{1}$. A measure with this
244	property is informationally complete (IC); one without is paracomplete (PC).
245	Plainly: does the measurement account for every possible outcome, or does it
246	leave some outcomes structurally unmeasured, not merely unmeasured for lack of
247	effort?
248	
249	\item \textbf{Symmetry.} The frame $\{M(E)\}$ may be symmetric ($S$),
250	asymmetric ($A$), or antisymmetric ($A^-$) under the pairing induced by the
251	frame operator. Plainly: is the set of possible outcomes balanced against
252	itself, lopsided, or exactly inverted?
253	
254	\item \textbf{Dynamics.} The assignment may be static or oscillating,
255	according to whether the relaxation time exceeds the observation window.
256	Plainly: does the measurement settle down, or does it keep changing no matter
257	how long you watch?
258	\end{itemize}
259	
260	These four axes give $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ cells, of which
261	oscillation drives the symmetric chirality onto the antisymmetric value, so
262	that symmetric-oscillating and antisymmetric-static coincide; twenty cells are
263	distinct. Every operator-valued measure, and on the claim of this paper every
264	theorem, lands in exactly one of these twenty cells.
265	
266	\subsection{One universal frame, many ordinary measures}
267	
268	The ambient structure is a single symmetric informationally complete
269	positive operator-valued measure, dual-framed and unary. Every object we
270	discuss is a measure \emph{with respect to that frame}, not another instance of
271	it. In particular the classification below assigns each theorem to a cell; a
272	theorem belongs to its cell, and not every inhabitant of the cell is that
273	theorem. Put differently: knowing a theorem's cell tells you its structural
274	family, the way knowing an animal's genus tells you a great deal without
275	telling you the species. The finer identity of each theorem is carried by
276	the twelve-coordinate encoding introduced next.
277	
278	\subsection{The twelve coordinates}
279	
280	Each object carries twelve coordinates. Nine of them are inert for the
281	classification; four carry the axes. This encoding is not built for this
282	paper; it is the standing twelve-primitive grammar used throughout the wider
283	catalog this work draws from, and the point of the next four rows is that
284	the twenty-four-cell classification above is not a new structure bolted onto
285	that grammar. It is already latent inside four of its twelve coordinates.
286	
287	\begin{center}
288	\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
289	\toprule
290	axis & coordinate & values \\
291	\midrule
292	Completeness & $\in$ & \sh{𐑔} complete; \sh{𐑚}, \sh{𐑲} paracomplete \\
293	Positivity & $\mdlgwhtsquare$ & \sh{𐑷} winding $0$; \sh{𐑴} winding $1/2$; \sh{𐑭} winding $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ \\
294	Dynamics & $\top$ & \sh{𐑧} static; \sh{𐑪} oscillating \\
295	Symmetry & $\succ$, $\bot$ & jointly, not separably \\
296	\bottomrule
297	\end{tabular}

299	
300	Positivity is carried by the winding coordinate alone, and in the winding unit
301	it is not a separate stipulation. This is the first substantial claim of the
302	paper, and the next subsection proves it rather than asserting it.
303	
304	\subsection{Positivity is a self-inverse winding}
305	
306	Before the proof, the picture it formalizes. A winding number counts how many
307	times a path circles around a point. If you reverse the direction of travel,
308	the count flips sign, \emph{except} at exactly two special values: winding
309	zero, where there is nothing to flip, and winding one-half, a half-turn,
310	where reversing the direction lands you back where you started. Those two
311	values are the only windings that are their own reverse. The claim below is
312	that this purely geometric fact --- which values survive reversal --- is
313	identical to the algebraic fact of whether a measurement is positive.
314	
315	Write $\wind{z} = \arg(z)/\omega \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ for the winding of a
316	nonzero complex number. A winding is \emph{self-inverse} when $x = -x$, which in
317	$\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ forces $2x \in \mathbb{Z}$ and hence $x \in \{0,
318	\tfrac12\}$; these are precisely the windings of the positive and the negative
319	reals.
320	
321	\begin{theorem}[positivity criterion]\label{thm:pos}
322	The three values of the winding coordinate are
323	\[
324	  \oint_\gamma dx = 0, \qquad
325	  \oint_\gamma A = \tfrac{n}{2}\,\omega \ (n \in \mathbb{Z}_2), \qquad
326	  \oint_\gamma A = n\,\omega \ (n \in \mathbb{Z},\ \wind{\gamma} \neq 0),
327	\]
328	with windings $0$, $1/2$ and $n$ respectively. The first two are exactly the
329	self-inverse windings; the third is exactly the winding that counts turns. The
330	measure is positive in the first two cases and not in the third.
331	\end{theorem}
332	
333	The classification therefore does not need positivity as an independent axis. A
334	measure is positive when its winding is a fixed point of negation --- equivalently,
335	when the quantity it accumulates around a cycle is real --- and negative when the
336	cycle deposits a count. Spectral flow through zero is what produces such a count,
337	which is why the negative case and the integer case coincide.
338	
339	\emph{Why this matters.} Positivity is normally imposed. One stipulates that the
340	operators of a measurement are positive because measurements are supposed to
341	return probabilities, and one checks the condition case by case. Theorem
342	\ref{thm:pos} replaces the stipulation with a fact about turns: go around the
343	cycle and see whether what you have gained is real. Nothing about probability is
344	assumed, and the two positive values are not two conventions but the only two
345	windings that reverse into themselves. An axis of the classification has become
346	a lemma about angles, which is a strictly stronger statement: it means
347	positivity was never a choice of convention in the first place, only a fact
348	about a picture that was there all along.

358	\subsection{Riemann}
359	
360	Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑥𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑠}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete,
361	negative, static.
362	
363	The parity coordinate is $\xi(s) = \xi(1-s)$: a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ action under
364	$s \mapsto 1-s$ leaving $\xi$ invariant, with $\mu \circ \delta = \mathrm{id}$.
365	The measurement coordinate is $[x,p] = i\hbar$, a self-adjoint operator whose
366	spectrum is $\{t : \xi(\tfrac12 + it) = 0\}$. The winding coordinate is
367	\[
368	  N(T) \;=\; \frac{1}{i\,\omega}\oint_\gamma \frac{\xi'}{\xi}\,ds
369	        \;=\; \wind{\xi}\big|_\gamma \;\in\; \mathbb{Z},
370	\]
371	the argument principle, which in this unit says directly that the zero count is
372	the winding of $\xi$ around the contour.
373	
374	Two coordinates of Riemann are the same self-inverse winding read twice. The
375	parity coordinate is the involution $s \mapsto 1-s$, whose winding is $1/2$; the
376	positivity coordinate is $\oint A = \tfrac{n}{2}\omega$, whose winding is $1/2$.
377	By Theorem \ref{thm:pos} the second is positive because the first is an
378	involution. Riemann is the only one of the seven whose functional equation and
379	whose positivity are the same fact --- which is a way of saying that the
380	symmetry everyone already knows about the zeta function is not merely
381	suggestive of the Hypothesis. It is, in this reading, algebraically the same
382	fact as the positivity the Hypothesis needs.
383	
384	The theorem asserts that the fixed locus of the parity coordinate contains every
385	zero counted by the winding coordinate.

388	
389	Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑥𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑵}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete,
390	negative, static. Nearest of the seven to the reference frame at distance
391	$0.6511$: of the seven, this is the one whose coordinates sit closest to a
392	proved object.

394	The measurement coordinate is Frobenius against Verschiebung on the Tate
395	module, $FV = p$, non-commuting. The winding coordinate is $\oint_\gamma A = n\,\omega$ with $n$ the regulator
396	index --- the determinant of the N\'eron--Tate height pairing on a basis of
397	$E(\mathbb{Q})/\mathrm{tors}$ --- a count, hence negative by Theorem

399	\[
400	  \operatorname{ord}_{s=1} L(E,s) \;=\; \operatorname{rank} E(\mathbb{Q}).
401	\]
402	In plain words: an analytic quantity (how fast an $L$-function vanishes at a
403	point) is claimed to equal an algebraic one (how many independent rational
404	points a curve has). The two look unrelated on the page; the classification
405	places them as two readings of the same winding coordinate.
406	
407	The corresponding \emph{question} carries stoichiometry $|A| = 1 \wedge |B| = 1$:
408	the unique bijection. That is the asserted rank equality, present as a
409	coordinate. As a theorem the coordinate moves to
410	$\exists a \in A\, \exists b \in B\, (\mathrm{type}(a) \neq \mathrm{type}(b))$:
411	two objects of different type, proved equal rather than identified.

438	\subsection{Navier--Stokes}
439	
440	Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑸𐑽𐑿𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑝𐑢𐑫𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete, negative,
441	static, and the only one of the seven off criticality.

443	The criticality coordinate is $\neg\exists \xi(\mathrm{diverges}\,\xi)$: no
444	diverging correlation length. That is global regularity,
445	$\sup_t \|u(t)\|_{H^s} < \infty$, which is the Millennium statement in full ---
446	plainly, the claim that a fluid obeying the Navier--Stokes equations never
447	develops a genuine singularity, no matter how long it is allowed to run.

449	coordinate. Of the seven problems in this paper, this is the cleanest case:

452	\subsection{P versus NP}
453	
454	Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑸𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑝}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete,
455	negative, static.

457	The measurement coordinate is nondeterministic branching against measurement of
458	the accepting path, which do not commute. The winding coordinate is an integer
459	that no continuous deformation removes: the separation. The question carries

463	equals NP starts from the most symmetric possible winding, and proving they
464	are different is exactly the act of that winding acquiring a nonzero count.

491	Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑸𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑲𐑵}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑴}$\rangle$; paracomplete,

507	\subsection{The measurement coordinate inverts}
508	
509	\begin{theorem}
510	All seven theorems carry measurement coordinate $[x,p] = i\hbar$. Six of the
511	seven corresponding questions carry $P(x) \in \{0,1\} \wedge \det(x)$.
512	\end{theorem}
513	
514	A Dirac measure assigns every event probability zero or one. The statement of a
515	problem is deterministic in this sense; its proof is not. In plain terms: the
516	\emph{question} each of these problems poses is phrased as though the answer
517	were already pinned down one way or the other, but the \emph{proof} that
518	would settle it has to work with genuinely non-commuting quantities. The
519	exception among the questions is Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, which carries a
520	mixed state $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2) < 1$: unlike the other six, its question
521	is already phrased in a form that admits partial, rather than all-or-nothing,
522	knowledge.
523	
524	\subsection{The measurement coordinate tracks criticality}\label{sec:grad}
525	
526	Over one hundred mathematical theorem coordinates, ninety-five carry
527	$[x,p] = i\hbar$ and five carry a Dirac measure or a mixed state. The
528	distribution of the five is not uniform.
529	
530	\begin{theorem}[criticality gradient]\label{thm:grad}
531	Let $\mathrm{gapped}$ denote the criticality value
532	$\neg\exists\xi(\mathrm{diverges}\,\xi)$. Among coordinates whose measurement is
533	not the commutator, seven of fourteen are gapped. Among those whose measurement
534	is the commutator, sixteen of one hundred and one are gapped. Equivalently: of
535	the coordinates at a critical point, ninety-two per cent are measured by a
536	commutator; of the gapped coordinates, seventy per cent are.
537	\end{theorem}
538	
539	A commutator is the measurement appropriate to a diverging correlation length,
540	where no finite scale separates the two quantities one wishes to fix. Away from
541	criticality that constraint is absent and a classical measurement suffices. In
542	plain terms: an object with no characteristic size forces you to measure two
543	things together, disturbing each by looking at the other; an object with a
544	finite scale lets you measure them one at a time. Four
545	of the five coordinates measured without a commutator ---
546	\texttt{simon\_problem\_classical}, \texttt{eden\_conjecture\_unproven},
547	\texttt{sic\_conjecture\_unproven}, \texttt{odd\_perfect} --- are gapped, and are
548	therefore measured as a gapped object permits.
549	
550	The gradient is not a rule. Sixteen gapped coordinates carry the commutator
551	regardless, among them Navier--Stokes, Goldbach, the Yang--Mills mass gap and
552	both formulations of the bounded Burnside problem.
553	
554	\emph{Why this matters.} It removes the choice of instrument from the
555	mathematician. If an object has no finite scale --- if its correlations reach
556	everywhere --- then the two things one wants to fix about it cannot be fixed
557	together, and any account of it that treats them as independently determinate is
558	describing a different object. The gradient says this is not a rule of thumb but
559	the ordinary case: of the coordinates at a critical point, ninety-two per cent
560	are measured by a commutator. Where a settled object was measured classically,
561	it was gapped and could afford to be. Put as advice rather than statistics: if
562	a problem you are working on is not gapped, expect that any proof strategy
563	which treats its two central quantities as separately fixable is fighting the
564	object rather than the mathematics.
565	
566	The fifth, \texttt{differentialadhesion}, sits at a critical point and is
567	measured by a mixed state. Its coordinates
568	$\langle$\sh{𐑨𐑰𐑩𐑬𐑞𐑧𐑚𐑝}$\odot$\sh{𐑖𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$ place it on a two-manifold
569	embedded in a continuum, with a strict order and a regular cardinal --- a
570	configuration shared with nothing else in the sample.
571	
572	\begin{observation}
573	\texttt{odd\_perfect} is the most inert coordinate in the sample: trivial
574	automorphism group, no critical point, a Dirac measure, and winding $0$. Nothing
575	accumulates around any cycle of it. In plain terms: it has no internal symmetry
576	to exploit, no sensitivity to nearby structure, and no self-consistent partial
577	information to leverage. It is, in this classification, the least structured
578	problem on the list, which is a different claim from being the easiest.
579	\end{observation}
