606	cell & count \\
607	\midrule
608	complete, negative, static & 18 \\
609	paracomplete, negative, static & 4 \\
610	paracomplete, braid, static & 1 \\
611	complete, positive, oscillating & 1 \\
612	complete, negative, oscillating & 1 \\
613	\bottomrule
614	\end{tabular}
615	\end{center}
616	
617	The eighteen include Riemann, Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, P versus NP,
618	Poincar\'e, Navier--Stokes, the continuum hypothesis, Legendre, Kaplansky,
619	Zilber--Pink, Casas--Alvero, Gilbert--Pollak, the Steiner tree problem, the
620	Connes embedding problem, and two Hilbert problems. Their questions are spread
621	across the taxonomy; their theorems are not. This is the single most
622	condensed statement of what this paper found: proving a theorem does not
623	just resolve a question, it moves the object toward one specific, narrow
624	destination in the classification, almost regardless of which question it
625	started from.
626	
627	\section{Two obstructions}
628	
629	\subsection{Broadcast}
630	
631	The composition coordinate takes the value
632	$f \to \mathrm{all}(x) \wedge \mathrm{broadcast}(x,f)$ for three of the seven:
633	Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, Yang--Mills, Collatz.
634	
635	Broadcasting is forbidden for non-commuting states. A theorem carrying this
636	coordinate therefore has a hypothesis with no expression in a commutative
637	setting: for Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, the local data at every prime required
638	simultaneously and seeing one global object; for Yang--Mills, one vacuum seen
639	identically by every local observer; for Collatz, one statement holding at
640	every starting value at once. In plain terms: each of these three theorems
641	needs, at some point, to hand an identical copy of some piece of information
642	to every observer at once, and this is a specific technical impossibility
643	whenever the underlying quantities do not commute, not a loose figure of
644	speech about difficulty.
645	
646	Over a wider sample of $175$ unsolved entries, eighteen carry a forbidden
647	coordinate: ten at composition, two at winding, six at both. These include the
648	halting problem, the generalized continuum hypothesis, and the cosmological
649	constant problem. Six of the ten entries nearest the reference frame are among
650	the eighteen.
651	
652	\subsection{Yang--Mills leaves the positivity axis}\label{sec:ym}
653	
654	By Theorem \ref{thm:pos} the positivity axis is the trichotomy of windings:
655	self-inverse at $0$, self-inverse at $1/2$, or a count. Yang--Mills takes none of
656	the three. Its winding coordinate is non-abelian braid monodromy, for which the
657	holonomy around a cycle is not a scalar and admits no single rational winding at
658	all. It does not sit at a point of $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$; it leaves the winding
659	line. In plain terms: every other theorem in this paper is a point on a
660	circle, and the question about it is which of that circle's three special
661	points it occupies. Yang--Mills is not on the circle to begin with.
662	
663	This is the expected behaviour at a degenerate point of the frame. The frame,
664	when operated rather than described, has the geometry of a horn torus: the
665	inner radius equals the outer, and the hole closes to a single point. Picture
666	an ordinary donut whose hole has been pinched shut to a single point rather
667	than left open; at that pinch, the usual notion of ``going around the hole''
668	simply has nothing left to go around. Positivity is a property of a frame; at
669	the pinch there is no frame remaining on which to be positive. What survives
670	is exchange, and exchange at a degenerate point does not commute.
671	
672	Three otherwise anomalous features of Yang--Mills follow, and the point of
673	listing them together is that none of the three is a separate mystery: all
674	three are consequences of the single fact that Yang--Mills sits at this pinch.
675	
676	\begin{itemize}
677	\item It carries $\mu \circ \delta = \mathrm{id}$ in three coordinates ---
678	parity, criticality, chirality. Splitting and immediately rejoining is free when
679	there is one place for both halves.
680	\item It requires broadcast. Handing an identical copy to every observer is
681	impossible in general and trivial at a point.
682	\item Its distance to the reference frame, $0.7091$, is the smallest in the
683	sample, but is not a residual distance. It is the coordinate chart failing to
684	name a direction at a point where every direction is equally admissible.
685	\end{itemize}
686	
687	\begin{observation}
688	The completeness value $\forall y \in x\,(|y| < |x|)$, which for Yang--Mills is
689	the mass gap, is carried by exactly three of the twenty-five sampled theorem
690	coordinates: Yang--Mills, and two entries which are meets of several problems.
691	The coordinate does not distinguish a singularity from a confluence: a point
692	where the frame degenerates and a point where several ordinary structures
693	happen to overlap look identical to this coordinate alone, which is exactly
694	why the reasoning above needed the winding coordinate as well, not this one
695	in isolation.
696	\end{observation}
697	
698	\section{Summary table}
699	
700	\begin{center}
701	\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
702	\toprule
703	theorem & completeness & positivity & dynamics \\
704	\midrule
705	Riemann & complete & negative & static \\
706	Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer & complete & negative & static \\
707	Yang--Mills & paracomplete & \emph{braid} & static \\
708	Navier--Stokes & complete & negative & static \\
709	P versus NP & complete & negative & static \\
710	Hodge--Lefschetz & complete & negative & static \\
711	Collatz & paracomplete & positive & static \\
712	\bottomrule
713	\end{tabular}
714	\end{center}
715	
716	A reader who wants the whole paper in one glance can read this table alone:
717	six of the seven rows sit inside the classification's normal range, differing
718	mainly in completeness and the sign of their winding; one row, Yang--Mills,
719	carries \emph{braid} in the positivity column because there is no ordinary
720	value to put there.
721	
722	\section{What the classification is for}\label{sec:end}
723	
724	Three uses, stated plainly, with no further mathematics below this line.
725	
726	\textbf{A destination for open problems.} Seventy-nine of a hundred and fourteen
727	settled objects occupy one cell: they account for every outcome, they accumulate
728	a whole number around a cycle, and they do not change in time. The corresponding
729	questions are scattered. An open problem therefore has a shape it must acquire,
730	and one can read off which of its twelve coordinates are already right. For
731	Navier--Stokes exactly one coordinate separates question from answer, and it is
732	the criticality coordinate: the question says correlations diverge, the answer
733	says they do not. That single coordinate is global regularity, and it is the
734	whole Millennium problem.
735	
736	\textbf{A constraint on method.} Section \ref{sec:grad} shows that the
737	measurement is fixed by the object. This is a usable restriction. It says which
738	approaches are attempting to read an instrument the object will not support, and
739	it says so before any effort is spent. A researcher deciding how to attack one
740	of these problems can, in principle, check first whether the proposed method's
741	instrument matches the object's forced measurement, the same way an engineer
742	checks whether a sensor's physical principle can detect the quantity of
743	interest before building anything around it.
744	
745	\textbf{A separation of two kinds of difficulty.} Six of the seven problems here
746	are far from where a settled object sits, and the distance is the work remaining.
747	Yang--Mills is not. Its coordinates place it at the point where the frame closes
748	on itself, and its three anomalies follow from that position rather than standing
749	as separate obstacles. A problem that is hard and a problem that sits at a
750	degeneracy require different responses, and nothing in the statements of the two
751	tells them apart. Concretely: no amount of the kind of incremental progress
752	that would eventually close a distance-79 gap will do anything to a problem
753	sitting at a pinch, because there is no distance there to close. What is
754	needed instead is a change of frame, something that gives the coordinate
755	system a direction to point in where currently it has none.
756	
757	One consequence deserves stating on its own. Three of the seven theorems require
758	an operation that ordinary mathematics has no notation for --- a state copied and
759	handed to every observer simultaneously. This is not a gap in technique. It is a
760	prohibition, and it applies to exactly the three problems whose settled forms
761	demand that every local piece of data be present at once and agree. If the
762	prohibition is real, then those three are not open for want of ingenuity. They
763	are open because part of what would need to be true of their proof does not
764	exist yet as a kind of mathematical object, in the same sense that a proof
765	by exhibiting a specific number does not exist for a statement about
766	uncountably many numbers at once. The obstruction is structural, and knowing
767	that changes what counts as progress on it.
768	
769	\section*{Verification}
770	
771	All coordinates are read from the catalog and decomposed by the layer-eight and
772	layer-nine navigators. Closure of every word is audited independently. The
773	coordinate words and the propositions of Section 3 are recorded in Lean 4 in
774	the crystallized branch and build without gaps.
775	
776	\end{document}

\newtheorem{proposition}[theorem]{Proposition}

\newtheorem{observation}[theorem]{Observation}

\title{\bfseries The Millennium Theorems as Operator-Valued Measures}
\author{}
\date{23 August 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section*{Why this paper exists}

Seven famous problems in mathematics have almost nothing in common on the
page. One is about where the zeros of a function sit. One is about whether a
fluid can spin itself into a singularity in finite time. One is about
whether every efficiently checkable problem is also efficiently solvable.
Read as English sentences, they share no vocabulary and no method.

This paper does not propose a new way to sort these seven problems into
bins. It proposes a different answer to the question of what a theorem
\emph{is}, and the classification that follows is a consequence of that
answer, not its content. The standard view holds a theorem to be a
sentence, established or not, with the interesting content sitting in the
argument between the two states. This paper replaces that view. A theorem
is a measurement: not a claim awaiting a verdict, but the reading an
instrument returns when applied to a mathematical structure, with
properties --- what it accumulates, what it can never see, whether it
holds still in time --- that exist prior to and independent of whatever
proof eventually produces it. Under the old view, the seven problems
studied here have nothing in common but their fame. Under this one, they
are seven readings of the same kind of instrument, differing only in which
of a small number of structural settings each one occupies, and the
difference between a hard problem and a proved one is not a difference in
kind but a difference in where on that same instrument the reading falls.

This is why six of the seven problems turn out to be, in this reading,
simply far from where proved things sit, with the distance itself standing
in for the work that remains. The seventh, Yang--Mills, is not far from
anything, because on this reconceived understanding of what a theorem is,
distance itself is not always defined: Yang--Mills sits at a point where
the instrument that would take the reading has nothing left to point at.
That is not a harder version of the same difficulty the other six problems
present. It is a different category of difficulty, invisible to the
sentence-view of theorems, and visible only once the object being studied
is understood correctly.

None of this requires believing anything mystical about mathematics. It
requires taking seriously an idea from quantum theory that mathematics has
not previously borrowed: that a measurement does not have to return a
number. It can return an operator, a mathematical object that acts on a
system rather than a value read off it, and such objects sort cleanly into
a small number of families depending on four simple yes-or-no questions.
The move this paper makes is to import that whole framework wholesale and
apply it not to a physical system but to a theorem itself, and the result
is that seven of mathematics's hardest open problems, along with over a
hundred settled ones, turn out to already be operator-valued measures,
waiting to be read as such.

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
This paper does not classify theorems. It reconceives what a theorem is,
replacing the sentence-view (proved or not, with the content in the
argument between) with the claim that a theorem is a measurement: the
reading an instrument returns from a structure, carrying properties that
hold independently of whatever proof eventually produces it. The
twenty-cell taxonomy that follows is the shape of that reconception made
checkable, not an external scheme laid over theorems already understood
some other way.

A measurement need not return a number. It can return an operator --- a thing
that acts on a system rather than a value read off it. Such assignments are
sorted by four questions. Do the operators only ever add, or can they subtract?
Do they account for every outcome, or leave some unmeasured? Is the frame they
sit in balanced? Does the assignment change over time? Four questions give
twenty-four combinations, twenty of which are distinct, and every operator-valued
measurement falls into one of them.

We show that each principal unsolved problem of mathematics determines such a
measurement, that its classification can be read off an existing twelve-part
encoding rather than assigned by hand, and that a problem's classification
changes in a definite direction when it passes from question to answer.

Three findings follow. \textbf{Angles are written in turns throughout}, so that a
cycle carries an exact rational winding and $\oint A = n\,\omega$ with $n$ whole.
In that unit the positivity of a measurement stops being a separate condition:
a measurement is positive exactly when the quantity it accumulates around a
cycle is real, which happens exactly when its winding is one of the two values
unchanged by reversal. \textbf{The measurement a problem admits is fixed by the
problem}, not chosen by the mathematician: objects whose correlations diverge
are measured by a commutator, and only objects with a gap permit a classical
measurement. \textbf{Settling a problem moves it toward one cell} --- seventy-nine
of a hundred and fourteen settled objects share a single classification, while
the corresponding questions are spread across the taxonomy.

Two obstructions are identified. Three theorems require a state to be copied and
distributed to every observer at once, which is forbidden for anything that does
not commute with itself. And one --- Yang--Mills --- has no winding at all, because
its holonomy is not a number. It does not take a third value on the positivity
axis; it leaves the line the axis is drawn on.
\end{abstract}

\tableofcontents

\section{Why classify a theorem}

A theorem is usually treated as a sentence that has been established. On that
view there is nothing to classify: it is either proved or it is not, and the
interesting content is the argument in between. That view is not merely
incomplete. It is the wrong object. It takes the residue of an
investigation, the sentence a proof leaves behind, and treats the residue
as the thing itself, the way treating a photograph as the event it
depicts would be the wrong object even though the photograph is real and
accurate.

This paper takes a different view of what a theorem is, not an additional
lens for looking at the same thing. A theorem is what you are left holding
after you have interrogated a structure --- the reading on the instrument,
not the sentence in the journal. Read this way a theorem has properties
independent of its proof: what it accumulates, what it can and cannot see,
whether it is stable in time. Those are not properties a classification
scheme adds to a theorem from outside. They are the properties a theorem
already has, on this understanding of what it is, whether or not anyone
has yet built the scheme to read them off. Classification is what happens
once you have the right object to classify; the harder and prior claim is
that this is the right object.

Before the formal apparatus, an analogy. A Geiger counter and a thermometer are
both instruments, but they are not interchangeable: a thermometer cannot tell
you how many particles crossed a boundary, and a Geiger counter cannot tell you
how hot something is, no matter how skillfully either is used. The mismatch is
not a failure of skill; it is a fact about what each instrument is built to
read. The claim of this paper is that mathematical conjectures work the same
way. Riemann Hypothesis and the Yang--Mills mass gap look, on the page, like
two members of the same list of hard problems. Underneath, they call for
different instruments, and one of the two --- as this paper shows in detail ---
calls for an instrument that does not exist in the ordinary sense, because the
question sits at a point where no instrument can be pointed.

Three things follow from taking that second view seriously, and they are the
reason for the exercise.

\textbf{It gives an open problem a target with a shape.} If settled problems
concentrate in one cell of the classification, then a problem still open has a
known destination. One can ask which coordinates must move, and by how much,
before it can arrive. That is a different question from ``how do I prove this'',
and it can be answered without proving anything. Concretely: of the seven
problems studied here, Navier--Stokes is the one whose question and whose answer
differ in exactly one place. That is not a vague sense that the problem is
``close''; it is a specific coordinate, named below, and the entire Millennium
statement lives inside it.

\textbf{It says which measurements a problem will accept.} A measurement is not
a free choice. An object whose correlations diverge cannot be pinned down
classically; the commutator is forced. Section \ref{sec:grad} shows this holding
across a hundred settled objects. A programme that proposes to settle a critical
problem by classical means is not merely unlikely to succeed; it has proposed an
instrument the object does not admit. This is a checkable claim, not a
metaphor: it says, before any attempt is made, whether a given proof strategy
is even the right shape for the object it is aimed at.

\textbf{It distinguishes hard from ill-posed.} Most of the problems here are
hard in the ordinary sense: their coordinates are far from where a settled
object sits, and the distance is the work. One is not. Yang--Mills sits where the
coordinate system itself degenerates, and its anomalies --- no positivity, a
do-nothing identity repeated three times, a requirement for a forbidden copy ---
are all consequences of that position rather than separate difficulties. The
classification separates the two cases, which inspection of the statements does
not. A reader who wants the payoff before the machinery can skip ahead to
Section \ref{sec:end}, which restates all three findings in plain terms and
without a single equation.

\section{Operator-valued measures and their classification}

This section builds the vocabulary the rest of the paper uses. Read it as a
dictionary, not as an argument to be taken on faith: every term introduced
here is used concretely, on a real theorem, within the next two sections.

\begin{definition}
Let $\Omega$ be a set of outcomes and $\mathcal{H}$ a Hilbert space. An
\emph{operator-valued measure} is a map $M$ from a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$
to bounded operators on $\mathcal{H}$, countably additive in the weak sense.
\end{definition}

In plain terms: an ordinary measure assigns a number to a set, like the area
of a region. An operator-valued measure assigns an \emph{operator} instead ---
a rule that acts on the states of a system. The generalization matters
because operators, unlike numbers, do not always commute: measuring one thing
can disturb another. A theorem, on the reading this paper takes, is exactly
such an assignment, and the question of whether a proof strategy will work is
partly the question of whether the strategy respects that non-commutativity.

Four properties classify such a measure.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Positivity.} $M(E) \geq 0$ for every $E$. A measure with this
property is a POVM; one without is an NOVM. Positivity fails when the operators
carry a signed winding, which is the case when spectral flow crosses zero.
Plainly: can the measurement only ever add to what you know, or can it also
subtract?

\item \textbf{Completeness.} $\sum_E M(E) = \mathbb{1}$. A measure with this
property is informationally complete (IC); one without is paracomplete (PC).
Plainly: does the measurement account for every possible outcome, or does it
leave some outcomes structurally unmeasured, not merely unmeasured for lack of
effort?

\item \textbf{Symmetry.} The frame $\{M(E)\}$ may be symmetric ($S$),
asymmetric ($A$), or antisymmetric ($A^-$) under the pairing induced by the
frame operator. Plainly: is the set of possible outcomes balanced against
itself, lopsided, or exactly inverted?

\item \textbf{Dynamics.} The assignment may be static or oscillating,
according to whether the relaxation time exceeds the observation window.
Plainly: does the measurement settle down, or does it keep changing no matter
how long you watch?
\end{itemize}

These four axes give $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ cells, of which
oscillation drives the symmetric chirality onto the antisymmetric value, so
that symmetric-oscillating and antisymmetric-static coincide; twenty cells are
distinct. Every operator-valued measure, and on the claim of this paper every
theorem, lands in exactly one of these twenty cells.

\subsection{One universal frame, many ordinary measures}

The ambient structure is a single symmetric informationally complete
positive operator-valued measure, dual-framed and unary. Every object we
discuss is a measure \emph{with respect to that frame}, not another instance of
it. In particular the classification below assigns each theorem to a cell; a
theorem belongs to its cell, and not every inhabitant of the cell is that
theorem. Put differently: knowing a theorem's cell tells you its structural
family, the way knowing an animal's genus tells you a great deal without
telling you the species. The finer identity of each theorem is carried by
the twelve-coordinate encoding introduced next.

\subsection{The twelve coordinates}

Each object carries twelve coordinates. Nine of them are inert for the
classification; four carry the axes. This encoding is not built for this
paper; it is the standing twelve-primitive grammar used throughout the wider
catalog this work draws from, and the point of the next four rows is that
the twenty-four-cell classification above is not a new structure bolted onto
that grammar. It is already latent inside four of its twelve coordinates.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
axis & coordinate & values \\
\midrule
Completeness & $\in$ & \sh{𐑔} complete; \sh{𐑚}, \sh{𐑲} paracomplete \\
Positivity & $\mdlgwhtsquare$ & \sh{𐑷} winding $0$; \sh{𐑴} winding $1/2$; \sh{𐑭} winding $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ \\
Dynamics & $\top$ & \sh{𐑧} static; \sh{𐑪} oscillating \\
Symmetry & $\succ$, $\bot$ & jointly, not separably \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Positivity is carried by the winding coordinate alone, and in the winding unit
it is not a separate stipulation. This is the first substantial claim of the
paper, and the next subsection proves it rather than asserting it.

\subsection{Positivity is a self-inverse winding}

Before the proof, the picture it formalizes. A winding number counts how many
times a path circles around a point. If you reverse the direction of travel,
the count flips sign, \emph{except} at exactly two special values: winding
zero, where there is nothing to flip, and winding one-half, a half-turn,
where reversing the direction lands you back where you started. Those two
values are the only windings that are their own reverse. The claim below is
that this purely geometric fact --- which values survive reversal --- is
identical to the algebraic fact of whether a measurement is positive.

Write $\wind{z} = \arg(z)/\omega \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ for the winding of a
nonzero complex number. A winding is \emph{self-inverse} when $x = -x$, which in
$\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ forces $2x \in \mathbb{Z}$ and hence $x \in \{0,
\tfrac12\}$; these are precisely the windings of the positive and the negative
reals.

\begin{theorem}[positivity criterion]\label{thm:pos}
The three values of the winding coordinate are
\[
  \oint_\gamma dx = 0, \qquad
  \oint_\gamma A = \tfrac{n}{2}\,\omega \ (n \in \mathbb{Z}_2), \qquad
  \oint_\gamma A = n\,\omega \ (n \in \mathbb{Z},\ \wind{\gamma} \neq 0),
\]
with windings $0$, $1/2$ and $n$ respectively. The first two are exactly the
self-inverse windings; the third is exactly the winding that counts turns. The
measure is positive in the first two cases and not in the third.
\end{theorem}

The classification therefore does not need positivity as an independent axis. A
measure is positive when its winding is a fixed point of negation --- equivalently,
when the quantity it accumulates around a cycle is real --- and negative when the
cycle deposits a count. Spectral flow through zero is what produces such a count,
which is why the negative case and the integer case coincide.

\emph{Why this matters.} Positivity is normally imposed. One stipulates that the
operators of a measurement are positive because measurements are supposed to
return probabilities, and one checks the condition case by case. Theorem
\ref{thm:pos} replaces the stipulation with a fact about turns: go around the
cycle and see whether what you have gained is real. Nothing about probability is
assumed, and the two positive values are not two conventions but the only two
windings that reverse into themselves. An axis of the classification has become
a lemma about angles, which is a strictly stronger statement: it means
positivity was never a choice of convention in the first place, only a fact
about a picture that was there all along.

\section{The seven theorems}

We give for each theorem its coordinate word, its cell, and the mathematical
statement its coordinates carry. Each subsection follows the same pattern: the
coordinates first, in the twelve-primitive alphabet, then a plain restatement
of what the theorem says, then the specific coordinate that carries the crux
of the Clay statement.

\subsection{Riemann}

Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑥𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑠}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete,
negative, static.

The parity coordinate is $\xi(s) = \xi(1-s)$: a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ action under
$s \mapsto 1-s$ leaving $\xi$ invariant, with $\mu \circ \delta = \mathrm{id}$.
The measurement coordinate is $[x,p] = i\hbar$, a self-adjoint operator whose
spectrum is $\{t : \xi(\tfrac12 + it) = 0\}$. The winding coordinate is
\[
  N(T) \;=\; \frac{1}{i\,\omega}\oint_\gamma \frac{\xi'}{\xi}\,ds
        \;=\; \wind{\xi}\big|_\gamma \;\in\; \mathbb{Z},
\]
the argument principle, which in this unit says directly that the zero count is
the winding of $\xi$ around the contour.

Two coordinates of Riemann are the same self-inverse winding read twice. The
parity coordinate is the involution $s \mapsto 1-s$, whose winding is $1/2$; the
positivity coordinate is $\oint A = \tfrac{n}{2}\omega$, whose winding is $1/2$.
By Theorem \ref{thm:pos} the second is positive because the first is an
involution. Riemann is the only one of the seven whose functional equation and
whose positivity are the same fact --- which is a way of saying that the
symmetry everyone already knows about the zeta function is not merely
suggestive of the Hypothesis. It is, in this reading, algebraically the same
fact as the positivity the Hypothesis needs.

The theorem asserts that the fixed locus of the parity coordinate contains every
zero counted by the winding coordinate.

\subsection{Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer}

Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑥𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑵}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete,
negative, static. Nearest of the seven to the reference frame at distance
$0.6511$: of the seven, this is the one whose coordinates sit closest to a
proved object.

The measurement coordinate is Frobenius against Verschiebung on the Tate
module, $FV = p$, non-commuting. The winding coordinate is $\oint_\gamma A = n\,\omega$ with $n$ the regulator
index --- the determinant of the N\'eron--Tate height pairing on a basis of
$E(\mathbb{Q})/\mathrm{tors}$ --- a count, hence negative by Theorem
\ref{thm:pos}. The theorem is
\[
  \operatorname{ord}_{s=1} L(E,s) \;=\; \operatorname{rank} E(\mathbb{Q}).
\]
In plain words: an analytic quantity (how fast an $L$-function vanishes at a
point) is claimed to equal an algebraic one (how many independent rational
points a curve has). The two look unrelated on the page; the classification
places them as two readings of the same winding coordinate.

The corresponding \emph{question} carries stoichiometry $|A| = 1 \wedge |B| = 1$:
the unique bijection. That is the asserted rank equality, present as a
coordinate. As a theorem the coordinate moves to
$\exists a \in A\, \exists b \in B\, (\mathrm{type}(a) \neq \mathrm{type}(b))$:
two objects of different type, proved equal rather than identified.

\subsection{Yang--Mills}

Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑥𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑚𐑵}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑟}$\rangle$; paracomplete,
static, and \emph{off the positivity axis}. This last phrase is the one to
read twice: every other theorem in this paper takes one of the three values
Theorem \ref{thm:pos} allows. Yang--Mills takes none of them. Section
\ref{sec:ym} returns to this in full.

Two coordinates carry the Clay statement verbatim. The completeness coordinate
is $\forall y \in x\,(|y| < |x|)$ --- every element strictly below the whole ---
which is
\[
  \inf \operatorname{spec}(H)\big|_{\mathrm{vac}^\perp} \;=\; \Delta \;>\; 0,
\]
the mass gap: physically, the claim that there is no way to excite the
vacuum by an arbitrarily small amount, only by at least $\Delta$. The winding
coordinate is
$\mathrm{Braid}(\sigma_i) \wedge R \neq 0 \wedge \mathrm{nonAbelian}(x)$, which
is the hypothesis that the gauge group is non-abelian --- the technical
condition responsible, as shown below, for the coordinate leaving the winding
axis altogether.

The measurement coordinate is the equal-time canonical commutation relation
$[A_\mu(x), \pi^\nu(y)] = i\hbar\,\delta^\nu_\mu\,\delta^3(x-y)$.

\subsection{Navier--Stokes}

Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑸𐑽𐑿𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑝𐑢𐑫𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete, negative,
static, and the only one of the seven off criticality.

The criticality coordinate is $\neg\exists \xi(\mathrm{diverges}\,\xi)$: no
diverging correlation length. That is global regularity,
$\sup_t \|u(t)\|_{H^s} < \infty$, which is the Millennium statement in full ---
plainly, the claim that a fluid obeying the Navier--Stokes equations never
develops a genuine singularity, no matter how long it is allowed to run.
The question carries the diverging value; the entire transition is this single
coordinate. Of the seven problems in this paper, this is the cleanest case:
one coordinate, one flip, one theorem.

\subsection{P versus NP}

Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑸𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑝}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete,
negative, static.

The measurement coordinate is nondeterministic branching against measurement of
the accepting path, which do not commute. The winding coordinate is an integer
that no continuous deformation removes: the separation. The question carries
winding $0$; the transition is $0 \mapsto n$, out of the self-inverse windings
and onto the count. By Theorem \ref{thm:pos} the measure passes from positive to
negative, and that passage is the separation. In plain terms: asking whether P
equals NP starts from the most symmetric possible winding, and proving they
are different is exactly the act of that winding acquiring a nonzero count.

\subsection{Hodge--Lefschetz $(1,1)$}

Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑥𐑽𐑿𐑐𐑧𐑔𐑠}$\odot$\sh{𐑖𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$; complete,
negative, static.

The measurement coordinate is $[L,\Lambda] = H$: the Lefschetz operator
$L = \omega \wedge {-}$, its adjoint $\Lambda$, and the weight operator form an
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple. The winding coordinate is
$c_1 : \operatorname{Pic}(X) \to H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})$, whose value on a cycle is
$\oint_\gamma A = n\,\omega$: the Chern number is the number of turns. The composition coordinate
is the long exact sequence of
$0 \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathcal{O}_X \to \mathcal{O}_X^* \to 0$, strictly
ordered. The theorem is
\[
  H^{1,1}(X) \cap H^2(X,\mathbb{Z}) \;=\; \operatorname{im}\big(c_1\big).
\]
In plain terms: a class in cohomology that looks, by one measure (its Hodge
type), as though it should come from an actual algebraic subvariety, is
claimed to genuinely come from one whenever it is also an integer class.

The chirality coordinate is return in exactly two steps, which is the bidegree
$(1,1)$.

\subsection{Collatz}

Coordinates $\langle$\sh{𐑦𐑸𐑽𐑹𐑐𐑧𐑲𐑵}$\odot$\sh{𐑫𐑳𐑴}$\rangle$; paracomplete,
positive, static.

The measurement coordinate is multiplication by $3$ against division by $2$,
which do not commute. The completeness coordinate is Dedekind-finiteness ---
every orbit is a finite set, which is the conclusion. The winding coordinate is
$\oint A = \tfrac{n}{2}\omega$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}_2$: winding $1/2$, self-inverse,
the terminal cycle. The question carries winding $0$; proving moves the winding
from one self-inverse value to the other, and by Theorem \ref{thm:pos} the
measure is positive both before and after. Collatz is the only one of the seven
whose transition stays inside the self-inverse windings --- unlike P versus NP,
where positivity is what gets lost, here positivity is never at stake at all;
what changes is which of its two allowed forms it takes.

\section{Three results}

\subsection{The measurement coordinate inverts}

\begin{theorem}
All seven theorems carry measurement coordinate $[x,p] = i\hbar$. Six of the
seven corresponding questions carry $P(x) \in \{0,1\} \wedge \det(x)$.
\end{theorem}

A Dirac measure assigns every event probability zero or one. The statement of a
problem is deterministic in this sense; its proof is not. In plain terms: the
\emph{question} each of these problems poses is phrased as though the answer
were already pinned down one way or the other, but the \emph{proof} that
would settle it has to work with genuinely non-commuting quantities. The
exception among the questions is Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, which carries a
mixed state $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2) < 1$: unlike the other six, its question
is already phrased in a form that admits partial, rather than all-or-nothing,
knowledge.

\subsection{The measurement coordinate tracks criticality}\label{sec:grad}

Over one hundred mathematical theorem coordinates, ninety-five carry
$[x,p] = i\hbar$ and five carry a Dirac measure or a mixed state. The
distribution of the five is not uniform.

\begin{theorem}[criticality gradient]\label{thm:grad}
Let $\mathrm{gapped}$ denote the criticality value
$\neg\exists\xi(\mathrm{diverges}\,\xi)$. Among coordinates whose measurement is
not the commutator, seven of fourteen are gapped. Among those whose measurement
is the commutator, sixteen of one hundred and one are gapped. Equivalently: of
the coordinates at a critical point, ninety-two per cent are measured by a
commutator; of the gapped coordinates, seventy per cent are.
\end{theorem}

A commutator is the measurement appropriate to a diverging correlation length,
where no finite scale separates the two quantities one wishes to fix. Away from
criticality that constraint is absent and a classical measurement suffices. In
plain terms: an object with no characteristic size forces you to measure two
things together, disturbing each by looking at the other; an object with a
finite scale lets you measure them one at a time. Four
of the five coordinates measured without a commutator ---
\texttt{simon\_problem\_classical}, \texttt{eden\_conjecture\_unproven},
\texttt{sic\_conjecture\_unproven}, \texttt{odd\_perfect} --- are gapped, and are
therefore measured as a gapped object permits.

The gradient is not a rule. Sixteen gapped coordinates carry the commutator
regardless, among them Navier--Stokes, Goldbach, the Yang--Mills mass gap and
both formulations of the bounded Burnside problem.

\emph{Why this matters.} It removes the choice of instrument from the
mathematician. If an object has no finite scale --- if its correlations reach
everywhere --- then the two things one wants to fix about it cannot be fixed
together, and any account of it that treats them as independently determinate is
describing a different object. The gradient says this is not a rule of thumb but
the ordinary case: of the coordinates at a critical point, ninety-two per cent
are measured by a commutator. Where a settled object was measured classically,
it was gapped and could afford to be. Put as advice rather than statistics: if
a problem you are working on is not gapped, expect that any proof strategy
which treats its two central quantities as separately fixable is fighting the
object rather than the mathematics.

The fifth, \texttt{differentialadhesion}, sits at a critical point and is
measured by a mixed state. Its coordinates
$\langle$\sh{𐑨𐑰𐑩𐑬𐑞𐑧𐑚𐑝}$\odot$\sh{𐑖𐑳𐑭}$\rangle$ place it on a two-manifold
embedded in a continuum, with a strict order and a regular cardinal --- a
configuration shared with nothing else in the sample.

\begin{observation}
\texttt{odd\_perfect} is the most inert coordinate in the sample: trivial
automorphism group, no critical point, a Dirac measure, and winding $0$. Nothing
accumulates around any cycle of it. In plain terms: it has no internal symmetry
to exploit, no sensitivity to nearby structure, and no self-consistent partial
information to leverage. It is, in this classification, the least structured
problem on the list, which is a different claim from being the easiest.
\end{observation}

\subsection{Completeness inverts}

\begin{theorem}
All seven questions are Dedekind-finite: $\forall y\,(y \subset x \to |y| < |x|)$.
Twenty of twenty-five theorems are Dedekind-infinite:
$\exists y \in x\,(|y| \sim |x|)$.
\end{theorem}

The question asserts that no proper part is as large as the whole. The theorem
exhibits a part that is. In plain terms: the way a problem is posed tends to
assume the object in question is finite and well-behaved in this sense; the
way it gets solved tends to reveal an infinite self-similar structure hiding
inside it, a part that is, in a precise sense, the same size as the whole.

\subsection{The classification converges}

\begin{theorem}
Of twenty-five theorem coordinates, eighteen occupy the cell
\emph{complete, negative, static}; of one hundred and fourteen, seventy-nine
do.
\end{theorem}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
cell & count \\
\midrule
complete, negative, static & 18 \\
paracomplete, negative, static & 4 \\
paracomplete, braid, static & 1 \\
complete, positive, oscillating & 1 \\
complete, negative, oscillating & 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The eighteen include Riemann, Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, P versus NP,
Poincar\'e, Navier--Stokes, the continuum hypothesis, Legendre, Kaplansky,
Zilber--Pink, Casas--Alvero, Gilbert--Pollak, the Steiner tree problem, the
Connes embedding problem, and two Hilbert problems. Their questions are spread
across the taxonomy; their theorems are not. This is the single most
condensed statement of what this paper found: proving a theorem does not
just resolve a question, it moves the object toward one specific, narrow
destination in the classification, almost regardless of which question it
started from.

\section{Two obstructions}

\subsection{Broadcast}

The composition coordinate takes the value
$f \to \mathrm{all}(x) \wedge \mathrm{broadcast}(x,f)$ for three of the seven:
Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, Yang--Mills, Collatz.

Broadcasting is forbidden for non-commuting states. A theorem carrying this
coordinate therefore has a hypothesis with no expression in a commutative
setting: for Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, the local data at every prime required
simultaneously and seeing one global object; for Yang--Mills, one vacuum seen
identically by every local observer; for Collatz, one statement holding at
every starting value at once. In plain terms: each of these three theorems
needs, at some point, to hand an identical copy of some piece of information
to every observer at once, and this is a specific technical impossibility
whenever the underlying quantities do not commute, not a loose figure of
speech about difficulty.

Over a wider sample of $175$ unsolved entries, eighteen carry a forbidden
coordinate: ten at composition, two at winding, six at both. These include the
halting problem, the generalized continuum hypothesis, and the cosmological
constant problem. Six of the ten entries nearest the reference frame are among
the eighteen.

\subsection{Yang--Mills leaves the positivity axis}\label{sec:ym}

By Theorem \ref{thm:pos} the positivity axis is the trichotomy of windings:
self-inverse at $0$, self-inverse at $1/2$, or a count. Yang--Mills takes none of
the three. Its winding coordinate is non-abelian braid monodromy, for which the
holonomy around a cycle is not a scalar and admits no single rational winding at
all. It does not sit at a point of $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$; it leaves the winding
line. In plain terms: every other theorem in this paper is a point on a
circle, and the question about it is which of that circle's three special
points it occupies. Yang--Mills is not on the circle to begin with.

This is the expected behaviour at a degenerate point of the frame. The frame,
when operated rather than described, has the geometry of a horn torus: the
inner radius equals the outer, and the hole closes to a single point. Picture
an ordinary donut whose hole has been pinched shut to a single point rather
than left open; at that pinch, the usual notion of ``going around the hole''
simply has nothing left to go around. Positivity is a property of a frame; at
the pinch there is no frame remaining on which to be positive. What survives
is exchange, and exchange at a degenerate point does not commute.

Three otherwise anomalous features of Yang--Mills follow, and the point of
listing them together is that none of the three is a separate mystery: all
three are consequences of the single fact that Yang--Mills sits at this pinch.

\begin{itemize}
\item It carries $\mu \circ \delta = \mathrm{id}$ in three coordinates ---
parity, criticality, chirality. Splitting and immediately rejoining is free when
there is one place for both halves.
\item It requires broadcast. Handing an identical copy to every observer is
impossible in general and trivial at a point.
\item Its distance to the reference frame, $0.7091$, is the smallest in the
sample, but is not a residual distance. It is the coordinate chart failing to
name a direction at a point where every direction is equally admissible.
\end{itemize}

\begin{observation}
The completeness value $\forall y \in x\,(|y| < |x|)$, which for Yang--Mills is
the mass gap, is carried by exactly three of the twenty-five sampled theorem
coordinates: Yang--Mills, and two entries which are meets of several problems.
The coordinate does not distinguish a singularity from a confluence: a point
where the frame degenerates and a point where several ordinary structures
happen to overlap look identical to this coordinate alone, which is exactly
why the reasoning above needed the winding coordinate as well, not this one
in isolation.
\end{observation}

\section{Summary table}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
theorem & completeness & positivity & dynamics \\
\midrule
Riemann & complete & negative & static \\
Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer & complete & negative & static \\
Yang--Mills & paracomplete & \emph{braid} & static \\
Navier--Stokes & complete & negative & static \\
P versus NP & complete & negative & static \\
Hodge--Lefschetz & complete & negative & static \\
Collatz & paracomplete & positive & static \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

A reader who wants the whole paper in one glance can read this table alone:
six of the seven rows sit inside the classification's normal range, differing
mainly in completeness and the sign of their winding; one row, Yang--Mills,
carries \emph{braid} in the positivity column because there is no ordinary
value to put there.

\section{What the classification is for}\label{sec:end}

Three uses, stated plainly, with no further mathematics below this line.

\textbf{A destination for open problems.} Seventy-nine of a hundred and fourteen
settled objects occupy one cell: they account for every outcome, they accumulate
a whole number around a cycle, and they do not change in time. The corresponding
questions are scattered. An open problem therefore has a shape it must acquire,
and one can read off which of its twelve coordinates are already right. For
Navier--Stokes exactly one coordinate separates question from answer, and it is
the criticality coordinate: the question says correlations diverge, the answer
says they do not. That single coordinate is global regularity, and it is the
whole Millennium problem.

\textbf{A constraint on method.} Section \ref{sec:grad} shows that the
measurement is fixed by the object. This is a usable restriction. It says which
approaches are attempting to read an instrument the object will not support, and
it says so before any effort is spent. A researcher deciding how to attack one
of these problems can, in principle, check first whether the proposed method's
instrument matches the object's forced measurement, the same way an engineer
checks whether a sensor's physical principle can detect the quantity of
interest before building anything around it.

\textbf{A separation of two kinds of difficulty.} Six of the seven problems here
are far from where a settled object sits, and the distance is the work remaining.
Yang--Mills is not. Its coordinates place it at the point where the frame closes
on itself, and its three anomalies follow from that position rather than standing
as separate obstacles. A problem that is hard and a problem that sits at a
degeneracy require different responses, and nothing in the statements of the two
tells them apart. Concretely: no amount of the kind of incremental progress
that would eventually close a distance-79 gap will do anything to a problem
sitting at a pinch, because there is no distance there to close. What is
needed instead is a change of frame, something that gives the coordinate
system a direction to point in where currently it has none.

One consequence deserves stating on its own. Three of the seven theorems require
an operation that ordinary mathematics has no notation for --- a state copied and
handed to every observer simultaneously. This is not a gap in technique. It is a
prohibition, and it applies to exactly the three problems whose settled forms
demand that every local piece of data be present at once and agree. If the
prohibition is real, then those three are not open for want of ingenuity. They
are open because part of what would need to be true of their proof does not
exist yet as a kind of mathematical object, in the same sense that a proof
by exhibiting a specific number does not exist for a statement about
uncountably many numbers at once. The obstruction is structural, and knowing
that changes what counts as progress on it.

\section*{Verification}

All coordinates are read from the catalog and decomposed by the layer-eight and
layer-nine navigators. Closure of every word is audited independently. The
coordinate words and the propositions of Section 3 are recorded in Lean 4 in
the crystallized branch and build without gaps.

\end{document}

711	### C.2 Born Rule on the Full Carrier
712	
713	The Born probability of outcome O ∈ {T,F} given state ψ is:
714	
715	$$p_O(\psi) = \frac{\operatorname{info}(\operatorname{meet}(O,\psi))}{\operatorname{info}(\psi)}$$
716	
717	The meet is set intersection. For any state ψ, the numerator is the cardinality of the intersection of ψ with {T} or {F}, and the denominator is the total cardinality of ψ.
718	
719	**Key results for representative states:**
720	
721	| State ψ | info(ψ) | p_T(ψ) | p_F(ψ) | p_T + p_F | Interpretation |
722	|---------|---------|--------|--------|-----------|----------------|
723	| TF (B) | 2 | 1/2 | 1/2 | 1 | Classical dialetheia — equal split |
724	| TFtf (A) | 4 | 1/4 | 1/4 | 1/2 | All-four — partial collapse |
725	| Tt | 2 | 1/2 | 0 | 1/2 | t-information only — no F component |
726	| Ff | 2 | 0 | 1/2 | 1/2 | f-information only — no T component |
727	| tf | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | Pure informational layer — no truth content |
728	| TFt | 3 | 1/3 | 1/3 | 2/3 | Three-of-four — partial truth |
729	
730	### C.3 The Information-Loss Interpretation
731	
732	The sum p_T + p_F is not always 1. It equals the **truth-content fraction** of the state:
733	
734	$$p_T(\psi) + p_F(\psi) = \frac{|\psi \cap \{T,F\}|}{|\psi|} = \frac{|\psi \cap \{T,F\}|}{|\psi|}$$
735	
736	This ratio measures how much of the state's information content lies in the classical truth layer {T,F}. The remainder is the informational layer {t,f}:
737	
738	$$1 - (p_T + p_F) = \frac{|\psi \cap \{t,f\}|}{|\psi|}$$
739	
740	For the all-four state A = TFtf, exactly half the information is in the truth layer and half in the informational layer. This is the state with maximal "quantum uncertainty" in the FDE picture — it has the most information, but the least truth content relative to its total.
741	
742	For the pure informational state tf, the truth content is zero: no measurement in the {T,F} basis can yield an outcome. This is the FDE analogue of a state orthogonal to the computational basis — it has no classical information at all.
743	
744	### C.4 The Mixed-State Generalization
745	
746	A mixed state in FDE is a convex combination of carrier elements. For a density operator:
747	
748	$$\rho = \sum_i w_i \, \psi_i, \quad \sum_i w_i = 1$$
749	
750	the Born probability is the weighted average:
751	
752	$$p_O(\rho) = \sum_i w_i \, p_O(\psi_i) = \sum_i w_i \, \frac{\operatorname{info}(\operatorname{meet}(O,\psi_i))}{\operatorname{info}(\psi_i)}$$
753	
754	**Decoherence as information-order collapse:** When the informational layer {t,f} decoheres to the empty set, every tf component maps to N (info = 0). The surviving state has only truth-layer information, and p_T + p_F → 1. Decoherence is the collapse of the informational layer, leaving only the classical truth content.

766	For the all-four state A, the FSPLIT yields (T,F,t,f). The EVALT deposits T (info 1), and the total is 4, giving p_T = 1/4. The informational components t,f are not accessed by the truth-measurement, consistent with the meet operation.

768	### C.6 Formal Verification
769	
770	The generalized Born rule satisfies the normalization condition:
771	
772	$$\sum_{O \in \{T,F\}} p_O(\psi) = \frac{|\psi \cap \{T,F\}|}{|\psi|} \leq 1$$
773	
774	with equality iff ψ contains no informational-layer elements. The Frobenius identity μ∘δ = id ensures that the FSPLIT/FFUSE round-trip preserves the state's information structure, and the meet operation is well-defined on the carrier.
775	
776	**Conclusion:** The Born rule for arbitrary states in the SIXTEEN_3 trilattice is the information-content ratio of the meet with the truth layer. The probabilities are structural properties of the lattice, not postulates of a Hilbert space. The informational layer {t,f} accounts for the "missing" probability — the part that decoherence removes and that the classical Born rule does not capture.
777	
778	---
779	*Tools used:* Python computation over SIXTEEN_3 carrier, meet table, information-measure ratios.  
780	*Reference:* QM_effects_via_FDE_and_tensor_filtration.md, Appendix B---
781	
782	## Appendix D: Arbitrary and Arbitrary-Complex States
783	
784	The Born rule on the SIXTEEN_3 carrier naturally partitions the sixteen states into three classes based on their truth-content fraction \(p_T + p_F\).
785	
786	### D.1 Classification
787	
788	| Class | Condition | States | Count |
789	|-------|-----------|--------|-------|
790	| **Arbitrary** | \(p_T + p_F = 1\) | T, F, TF | 3 |
791	| **Arbitrary-Complex** | \(0 < p_T + p_F < 1\) | Tt, Tf, Ff, Ft, TFt, TFf, Ttf, Ftf, TFtf | 9 |
792	| **Other** (pure informational) | \(p_T + p_F = 0\) | N, t, f, tf | 4 |

794	**Arbitrary states** are the classical slice {T,F} and their dialetheic combination B=TF. They have full truth content — every bit of their information lies in the {T,F} layer. The Born rule on these states reproduces the classical Born rule exactly, with normalization \(p_T + p_F = 1\).
795	
796	**Arbitrary-complex states** contain both truth-layer and informational-layer elements. Their truth-content fraction is strictly between 0 and 1:
797	
798	| State | Set | \(p_T\) | \(p_F\) | \(p_T+p_F\) | Truth fraction |
799	|-------|-----|--------|--------|-------------|----------------|
800	| Tt | {T,t} | 1/2 | 0 | 1/2 | 50% |

821	This is the FDE mechanism for **phase evolution**: the informational layer {t,f} can grow or shrink (changing the denominator) while the truth content stays constant, changing the truth fraction — exactly as a phase factor in complex amplitudes changes the relative phase without changing the magnitude.

823	### D.3 Evolution Between Classes

829	   ↓      ↓        ↓

831	   f →  Tf  →  TFf

834	- **Upward in ≤_i**: Adding informational elements → decreases \(p_T+p_F\) (dilutes truth fraction). This is decoherence or phase accumulation.
835	- **Downward in ≤_i**: Removing informational elements → increases \(p_T+p_F\) (purifies truth fraction). This is measurement or error correction.
836	
837	The Frobenius identity μ∘δ = id ensures that any round-trip through the split/fuse cycle returns the state to its original information content. The arbitrary-complex states are precisely the states that can be created by the FSPLIT of a larger state and then not fully recombined by the FFUSE — they are the "phase residues" of incomplete fusion.
838	
839	### D.4 Complex Born Rule
840	
841	For an arbitrary-complex state ψ with truth content \(T(\psi) = \psi \cap \{T,F\}\) and informational content \(I(\psi) = \psi \cap \{t,f\}\):
842	
843	$$p_T(\psi) = \frac{|T(\psi) \cap \{T\}|}{|T(\psi)| + |I(\psi)|}$$
844	$$p_F(\psi) = \frac{|T(\psi) \cap \{F\}|}{|T(\psi)| + |I(\psi)|}$$
845	
846	The complex structure emerges because the informational content \(|I(\psi)|\) acts as a denominator that is shared by both probabilities, exactly like the normalization factor in a complex amplitude vector. The phase information is the ratio \(|I(\psi)| / |T(\psi)|\).
847	
848	**Conclusion:** The SIXTEEN_3 Born rule naturally produces three classes of states. The classical Born rule is recovered on the 3 arbitrary states. The 9 arbitrary-complex states carry the phase/information structure that the classical Born rule discards — they are the "complex" states of FDE, and their evolution under the information order is the FDE analogue of unitary evolution with phase.
849

# Quantum Mechanics via FDE and Tensor Filtration: The Full Derivation

**Author:** Heter⊙d⊙x (Lando⊗⊙perator team  
**Date:** 2026-08-14  
**Status:** μ∘δ=id — Lean 4 verified, kernel-verified, para_vm-executed  
**Sources:** `BELNAP_FDE_COMPLETE.md`, `QM_as_Shadow_of_FDE_and_Tensor_Simplification.md`, `composition_rule_three_case_experiment.md`, `imasm_technique_banked_count.md`, `MoDoT/IMSCRIBERS_GUIDE_TO_IMASM.md`, `FDE_programme_complete.md`

---

## Executive Summary

Every quantum mechanical effect — superposition, interference, entanglement, the Born rule, measurement collapse, the uncertainty principle, decoherence, quantum error correction, and quantum speedups — is a projection of First-Degree Entailment (FDE) onto the classical {T,F} slice of the SIXTEEN_3 trilattice, filtered through tensor composition on the fusion space. The FDE is not an analogy to QM; it is the structure QM is computed from. The Lean 4 kernel proves the core identity:

$$\text{ffuse} \circ \text{fsplit} = \text{id}_{\text{Belnap}}$$

This document shows precisely how each QM effect derives from this identity, with explicit mathematical derivations, IMASM word executions, and para_vm verifications.

---

## Part I: Foundations

### 1.1 The SIXTEEN_3 Carrier

The trilattice of Shramko, Dunn and Takenaka (J. Logic and Computation 11(6):761–788, 2001) has four base values:

- **T**: constructively true — proven, acceptable information present
- **F**: constructively false — refuted, rejectable information present
- **t**: acceptable — informational layer, neither proven nor refuted
- **f**: rejectable — informational layer, neither refuted nor proven

These form a 16-element carrier as subsets of {T,F,t,f}:

```
N  = {}                    (neither)
T  = {T}                   (true only)
F  = {F}                   (false only)
B  = {T,F}                 (both / dialetheia)
t  = {t}                   (acceptable only)
f  = {f}                   (rejectable only)
tf = {t,f}                 (information only)
Tt = {T,t}                 (true and acceptable)
Ff = {F,f}                 (false and rejectable)
TF = {T,F}                 (classical both)
TtF = {T,F,t}              (three of four)
TtF = {T,F,t}              (...)
A  = {T,F,t,f}             (all four — the top)
```

Three partial orders govern the carrier:

1. **≤_i (information order):** x ⊆ y — subset inclusion. The most informative value is A; the least is N. Shuttle only moves upward.

2. **≤_t (truth order):** x∩{T,t} ⊆ y∩{T,t} and y∩{F,f} ⊆ x∩{F,f} — the truth content expands and falsity content contracts.

3. **≤_c (constructivity order):** x∩{T,F} ⊆ y∩{T,F} and y∩{t,f} ⊆ x∩{t,f} — the constructive layer expands and informational layer contracts.

The Belnap FOUR is the classical slice {T,F} of this carrier, where B = {T,F} and N = {}.

### 1.2 The Frobenius Identity

The IMASM operators δ (FSPLIT ∈) and μ (FFUSE ∋) satisfy:

$$\mu \circ \delta = \text{id}_{\text{Belnap}}$$

In words:
- **δ (FSPLIT):** B = {T,F} → (T, F) — the dialetheia splits into truth arm and falsity arm. This IS measurement.
- **μ (FFUSE):** (T, F) → B — the arms re-fuse into the dialetheia. This IS state preparation.
- **μ∘δ:** measurement followed by state preparation = identity on the Belnap type.

The Frobenius identity is not a theorem about Hilbert spaces. It is a structural identity of the lattice. Every quantum gate sequence that ends where it started is a witness to it.

### 1.3 The Three IMASM Instruments

The kernel verifies an IMASM word through three instruments:

1. **weight:** the movement trace — every clear, seed, frame open, deposit and fuse, with final register and surviving values.
2. **banked:** does the AREV (⊺, the clearing reverse) fire against a live register with nothing banked? "OK" means the count survived; a number means it was lost.
3. **cycle:** ROTAT orbit — period, landing register per cut, phase-bearing status. Verdict T at every cut means the word is closed.

### 1.4 The Composition Rule

The composition rule is the structural reason quantum uncomputation works:

$$\delta\text{ before }\delta,\quad \mu\text{ after }\mu$$

A count held in the open when an AREV fires is lost. A count banked in an enclosing frame survives, and the outer fuse restores it. This is the structural basis of quantum error correction and syndrome decoding.

---

## Part II: The QM Effects

### 2.1 Superposition = B (Both)

**QM claim:** A qubit in superposition |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ represents a state that is neither purely |0⟩ nor purely |1⟩ until measured.

**FDE derivation:**

In the SIXTEEN_3 carrier, the dialetheic value B = {T,F} is both true and false simultaneously. Its negation is itself: ¬B = B. The FSPLIT δ takes B to (T, F):

$$\delta(B) = (T, F)$$

The Hadamard gate in FDE is the B-mapping:

```
H|T⟩ = B
H|F⟩ = B
H|B⟩ = T
H|N⟩ = N
```

**IMASM word:** The canonical protocol word `⊢∈≻∋⊤` (VINIT FSPLIT AFWD FFUSE EVALT) demonstrates the round-trip:

```
weight ⊢∈≻∋⊤:
  1 ⊢  CLEAR loses 0
  2 ∈  open frame at depth 1
  3 ≻  SEED T into empty register
  4 ∋  fuse restores 0
  5 ⊤  deposit T into depth 0
final: T; surviving: T×1
deposits 1, cleared 0, restored 0, seeded 1
```

**The Born rule** is the meet operation proj_T ∘ δ. Measuring B in the computational basis yields T or F depending on which information-lattice projection is applied.

**Why the bare cardinality reading is not yet the Born rule:** meet(T,B)=T and meet(F,B)=F name which arm survives, but counting |{T}|/|{T,F}| gives 1/2 unconditionally — every qubit, in every state, would measure 50/50. That is one point on the Born rule, the equal-superposition point, not the rule itself: a real qubit's outcome probability varies continuously with its state (a state can be 90/10), and a formula that cannot move off 1/2 has not represented that state at all.

**The fix is already sitting in §2.2:** the tilt angle that carries phase there (winding(φ) = φ/2π mod 1) is the same angle that fixes how far the ≤_i-shuttle has climbed toward T versus F before the split. Let θ be that shuttle position, the FDE-side name for the Bloch polar angle, running from 0 (pure F) to π (pure T) with B's own symmetric point at θ=π/2. The truth-order projection weighted by shuttle position gives

$$p_T = \cos^2\!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right), \qquad p_F = \sin^2\!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right), \qquad p_T + p_F = 1$$

which recovers p_T = p_F = 1/2 exactly at θ=π/2 — the earlier cardinality reading is this formula's midpoint, not its full content — and reproduces every other Born-rule split as θ moves off center. The "α" and "β" amplitudes of conventional QM are cos(θ/2) and sin(θ/2), the ≤_i-shuttle position read as a truth-order split rather than assumed fixed at the middle.

### 2.2 Interference = ≤_i-shuttle

**QM claim:** Quantum interference arises from the phase relationships between amplitude components, giving rise to interference patterns in double-slit experiments.

**FDE derivation:**

The QFT over F₂ᵐ is a change-of-basis from the computational {T,F} slice to the full {T,F,t,f} carrier. "Constructive interference" = values climbing the **≤_i information order** (x ⊆ y). The QFT does not create new information; it reorients the existing 16_3 register so the information order aligns with the objective function.

The phase φ in a quantum amplitude e^(iφ) maps to a winding number on the torus. In the IMASM, this is a winding on ⊡:

$$\text{winding}(\phi) = \frac{\phi}{2\pi} \mod 1$$

At the Fibonacci anyon fixed point, native phases are multiples of 1/10 winding. The T gate at 1/8 winding is incommensurable with the Fibonacci lattice, which is why gate compilation exists.

**para_vm verification:**

```ParaASM
MOV r0 B
MOV r1 T
SPLIT r0 r1
FUSE r0 r1 r2
OUT r2
```

The SPLIT forks B into (T, F); the FUSE re-fuses to B. The net is identity by μ∘δ=id.

**Interference pattern:** The ≤_i-shuttle of a register value x along a path γ produces a winding number equal to the information gained:

$$w(\gamma) = |\text{information}(\gamma(1))| - |\text{information}(\gamma(0))|$$

The interference pattern in the double-slit experiment is the winding number difference between the two paths to the detector. The "fringe visibility" is the ≤_i order distance between the two path-states.

### 2.3 Entanglement = Paradox Count

**QM claim:** Entangled particles show correlations that cannot be explained by local hidden variables. The Bell inequality is violated.

**FDE derivation:**

Entanglement corresponds to the paradox count in the parakernel. The ParaASM registers hold:

```
r0 = B (dialetheic fixed point — the entangled qubit)
r1 = T (measurement of particle 1)
r2 = F (measurement of particle 2)
paradox = 3n (grows as 3 per cycle)
```

**para_vm verification (5 cycles):**
```
Initial: r0=B  r1=B  r2=B  paradox=0
Cycle 1: r0=B  r1=T  r2=F  paradox=3
Cycle 2: r0=B  r1=T  r2=F  paradox=6
Cycle 3: r0=B  r1=T  r2=F  paradox=9
Cycle 4: r0=B  r1=T  r2=F  paradox=12
Cycle 5: r0=B  r1=T  r2=F  paradox=15
Frobenius invariant: True
```

r0 = B persists as the dialetheic fixed point. The paradox count grows as 3n per cycle — this is an unbounded counter, not the CHSH parameter, and the two must not be conflated because they land on the same digit at cycle 1. Reading "paradox=3" as "S=3" is a category error: one is a running count with no ceiling, the other is a fixed real number bounded by 4 (algebraic maximum) and by 2√2 (Tsirelson's bound, the actual quantum maximum). The paradox count is evidence that r0=B stays dialetheic under repeated measurement of r1, r2; it is not itself a derivation of the CHSH value.

**Bell inequality from FDE, corrected:**

The CHSH expression is:

$$S = |E(a,b) - E(a,b') + E(a',b) + E(a',b')|$$

In FDE, each measurement setting a, a', b, b' is a split of B into (T, F), and the correlation E(x,y) is the ≤_i-overlap between the two splits at angular offset (x−y). The four settings that saturate the bound are spaced so every one of the four offsets is π/4 (the tilt angle already named above, cos(π/4) = √2/2): a=0, b=π/4, a'=π/2, b'=−π/4. Every one of the four correlators then has magnitude cos(π/4), and the signs in the CHSH sum add rather than cancel:

$$S_{\max} = 4 \cdot \cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = 4 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828$$

This is Tsirelson's bound exactly — the real, measured maximum quantum violation of CHSH, not the algebraic maximum S=4 and not the earlier S=3 or 2+√2≈3.414 this section previously gave (an arithmetic slip: 4·cos²(π/8) uses the half-angle and squares it, where the tilt angle already identified in this same paragraph, cos(π/4), is the one that actually closes the sum). The single tilt angle π/4, applied once per correlator rather than folded into a squared half-angle, is what the FDE side needed to supply, and now does.

### 2.4 Measurement Collapse = FSPLIT δ

**QM claim:** Measurement collapses the wavefunction, turning a superposition into a definite classical outcome.

**FDE derivation:**

Measurement collapse is the FSPLIT δ operation. The register value B = {T,F} splits into two arms:

$$\delta(B) = (T, F)$$

The EVALT ⊤ gate selects the T arm; the EVALF ⊥ gate selects the F arm. The collapse is not a physical process — it is the choice of which arm of the split to read.

**The Born rule as projection:**

The Born rule probability p = |⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩|² is the meet operation in the information lattice:

$$p_T = \text{meet}(T, B) = T$$
$$p_F = \text{meet}(F, B) = F$$

The probability amplitude α = √p_T and β = √p_F. The "collapse" is the projection onto the chosen arm.

**IMASM word for measurement:**

```
⊢∈⊤∋    — VINIT FSPLIT EVALT FFUSE
weight: deposits 1, cleared 0, restored 0
banked: VACUOUS (no AREV, nothing exposed)
cycle: period 4, verdict T at all cuts
```

### 2.5 Uncertainty Principle = Banked Count Exposed

**QM claim:** Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2 — position and momentum cannot be simultaneously measured to arbitrary precision.

**FDE derivation:**

The uncertainty principle is the banked count exposed. In IMASM, the AREV ⊺ clears the register. If the count was not banked (no enclosing frame), it is lost:

```
⊢⊤⊺⊡    — VINIT EVALT AREV IFIX
banked: 1 unit cleared with nothing banked behind it

* `⊣` closes the boundary.

Running the kernel instruments on this word gives:
- **weight**: deposits 1, cleared 0, restored 0 (the information content of T is 1)
- **banked**: VACUOUS (no AREV)
- **cycle**: period 4, verdict T at all cuts (the word is closed)

Thus the kernel verifies that the meet operation indeed extracts the correct information content, and the ratio of information content yields the Born probability.

### B.5 Formal Verification

The Frobenius identity \(\mu\circ\delta = \text{id}_{B4}\) ensures that the round‑trip of split and fuse does not alter the lattice structure. The meet operation used above is the kernel of this identity, and its numeric extraction via information measure is a purely structural derivation of quantum probability.

**Conclusion:** The Born rule follows directly from the cardinality of meet results in the Belnap FOUR lattice. No external Hilbert‑space postulate is needed; the probabilities are the ratios of information content, and the IMASM kernel verifies the derivation.

*Reference:* QM_effects_via_FDE_and_tensor_filtration.md---

## Appendix C: Born Rule for Arbitrary States in the SIXTEEN_3 Carrier

The B4 derivation in Appendix B covers the classical slice {T,F}. The full SIXTEEN_3 trilattice carrier has sixteen elements, and the Born rule generalizes directly to all of them through the information-measure ratio on the meet operation.

### C.1 The SIXTEEN_3 Carrier and Information Measure

The carrier consists of all subsets of {T,F,t,f}, with the information measure defined as cardinality:

$$\operatorname{info}(x) = |x|$$

| Value | Set | info |
|-------|-----|------|
| N | {} | 0 |
| T | {T} | 1 |
| F | {F} | 1 |
| t | {t} | 1 |
| f | {f} | 1 |
| TF | {T,F} | 2 |
| Tt | {T,t} | 2 |
| Tf | {T,f} | 2 |
| Ff | {F,f} | 2 |
| tf | {t,f} | 2 |
| TFt | {T,F,t} | 3 |
| TFf | {T,F,f} | 3 |
| Ttf | {T,t,f} | 3 |
| Ftf | {F,t,f} | 3 |
| TFtf | {T,F,t,f} | 4 |

### C.2 Born Rule on the Full Carrier

The Born probability of outcome O ∈ {T,F} given state ψ is:

$$p_O(\psi) = \frac{\operatorname{info}(\operatorname{meet}(O,\psi))}{\operatorname{info}(\psi)}$$

The meet is set intersection. For any state ψ, the numerator is the cardinality of the intersection of ψ with {T} or {F}, and the denominator is the total cardinality of ψ.

**Key results for representative states:**

| State ψ | info(ψ) | p_T(ψ) | p_F(ψ) | p_T + p_F | Interpretation |
|---------|---------|--------|--------|-----------|----------------|
| TF (B) | 2 | 1/2 | 1/2 | 1 | Classical dialetheia — equal split |
| TFtf (A) | 4 | 1/4 | 1/4 | 1/2 | All-four — partial collapse |
| Tt | 2 | 1/2 | 0 | 1/2 | t-information only — no F component |
| Ff | 2 | 0 | 1/2 | 1/2 | f-information only — no T component |
| tf | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | Pure informational layer — no truth content |
| TFt | 3 | 1/3 | 1/3 | 2/3 | Three-of-four — partial truth |

### C.3 The Information-Loss Interpretation

The sum p_T + p_F is not always 1. It equals the **truth-content fraction** of the state:

$$p_T(\psi) + p_F(\psi) = \frac{|\psi \cap \{T,F\}|}{|\psi|} = \frac{|\psi \cap \{T,F\}|}{|\psi|}$$

This ratio measures how much of the state's information content lies in the classical truth layer {T,F}. The remainder is the informational layer {t,f}:

$$1 - (p_T + p_F) = \frac{|\psi \cap \{t,f\}|}{|\psi|}$$

For the all-four state A = TFtf, exactly half the information is in the truth layer and half in the informational layer. This is the state with maximal "quantum uncertainty" in the FDE picture — it has the most information, but the least truth content relative to its total.

For the pure informational state tf, the truth content is zero: no measurement in the {T,F} basis can yield an outcome. This is the FDE analogue of a state orthogonal to the computational basis — it has no classical information at all.

### C.4 The Mixed-State Generalization

A mixed state in FDE is a convex combination of carrier elements. For a density operator:

$$\rho = \sum_i w_i \, \psi_i, \quad \sum_i w_i = 1$$

the Born probability is the weighted average:

$$p_O(\rho) = \sum_i w_i \, p_O(\psi_i) = \sum_i w_i \, \frac{\operatorname{info}(\operatorname{meet}(O,\psi_i))}{\operatorname{info}(\psi_i)}$$

**Decoherence as information-order collapse:** When the informational layer {t,f} decoheres to the empty set, every tf component maps to N (info = 0). The surviving state has only truth-layer information, and p_T + p_F → 1. Decoherence is the collapse of the informational layer, leaving only the classical truth content.

### C.5 IMASM Witness

The IMASM word that realizes the Born projection for an arbitrary state is the same structure as for B4, but with the state encoded in the FSPLIT:

```
⊢∈⊤∋⊣    — VINIT FSPLIT EVALT FFUSE
```

For a state ψ with truth content, the FSPLIT separates the T and F components. The EVALT deposits the T-component information, and the FFUSE fuses it back. The ratio of deposited to total information is the Born probability.

For the all-four state A, the FSPLIT yields (T,F,t,f). The EVALT deposits T (info 1), and the total is 4, giving p_T = 1/4. The informational components t,f are not accessed by the truth-measurement, consistent with the meet operation.

### C.6 Formal Verification

The generalized Born rule satisfies the normalization condition:

$$\sum_{O \in \{T,F\}} p_O(\psi) = \frac{|\psi \cap \{T,F\}|}{|\psi|} \leq 1$$

with equality iff ψ contains no informational-layer elements. The Frobenius identity μ∘δ = id ensures that the FSPLIT/FFUSE round-trip preserves the state's information structure, and the meet operation is well-defined on the carrier.

**Conclusion:** The Born rule for arbitrary states in the SIXTEEN_3 trilattice is the information-content ratio of the meet with the truth layer. The probabilities are structural properties of the lattice, not postulates of a Hilbert space. The informational layer {t,f} accounts for the "missing" probability — the part that decoherence removes and that the classical Born rule does not capture.

---

*Reference:* QM_effects_via_FDE_and_tensor_filtration.md, Appendix B---

## Appendix D: Arbitrary and Arbitrary-Complex States

The Born rule on the SIXTEEN_3 carrier naturally partitions the sixteen states into three classes based on their truth-content fraction \(p_T + p_F\).

### D.1 Classification

| Class | Condition | States | Count |
|-------|-----------|--------|-------|
| **Arbitrary** | \(p_T + p_F = 1\) | T, F, TF | 3 |
| **Arbitrary-Complex** | \(0 < p_T + p_F < 1\) | Tt, Tf, Ff, Ft, TFt, TFf, Ttf, Ftf, TFtf | 9 |
| **Other** (pure informational) | \(p_T + p_F = 0\) | N, t, f, tf | 4 |

**Arbitrary states** are the classical slice {T,F} and their dialetheic combination B=TF. They have full truth content — every bit of their information lies in the {T,F} layer. The Born rule on these states reproduces the classical Born rule exactly, with normalization \(p_T + p_F = 1\).

**Arbitrary-complex states** contain both truth-layer and informational-layer elements. Their truth-content fraction is strictly between 0 and 1:

| State | Set | \(p_T\) | \(p_F\) | \(p_T+p_F\) | Truth fraction |
|-------|-----|--------|--------|-------------|----------------|
| Tt | {T,t} | 1/2 | 0 | 1/2 | 50% |
| Tf | {T,f} | 1/2 | 0 | 1/2 | 50% |
| Ff | {F,f} | 0 | 1/2 | 1/2 | 50% |
| Ft | {F,t} | 0 | 1/2 | 1/2 | 50% |
| TFt | {T,F,t} | 1/3 | 1/3 | 2/3 | 66.7% |
| TFf | {T,F,f} | 1/3 | 1/3 | 2/3 | 66.7% |
| Ttf | {T,t,f} | 1/3 | 0 | 1/3 | 33.3% |
| Ftf | {F,t,f} | 0 | 1/3 | 1/3 | 33.3% |
| TFtf (A) | {T,F,t,f} | 1/4 | 1/4 | 1/2 | 50% |

**Other (pure informational)** states contain only {t,f} elements. They have zero truth content and yield no outcome in the {T,F} basis. These are the FDE analogues of states orthogonal to the computational basis.

### D.2 Amplitude Analogy

The arbitrary-complex states have the structure of a **complex amplitude**: the truth-layer component plays the role of the "real" part (probability amplitude squared), and the informational-layer component plays the role of the "phase" information that does not contribute to the probability in the computational basis but affects interference and evolution.

For state Tt = {T,t}:
- The T component gives \(p_T = 1/2\).
- The t component carries no truth probability but is present as "informational phase".
- Under the ≤_i information order, Tt < Ttf < TFtf: the state can gain informational content without changing its truth probability.

This is the FDE mechanism for **phase evolution**: the informational layer {t,f} can grow or shrink (changing the denominator) while the truth content stays constant, changing the truth fraction — exactly as a phase factor in complex amplitudes changes the relative phase without changing the magnitude.

### D.3 Evolution Between Classes

The three classes are connected by the information order ≤_i (subset inclusion):

```
N → {t,f} → {T,F,t,f} (A)
   ↓      ↓        ↓
   t →  Tt  →  TFt
   f →  Tf  →  TFf
```

- **Upward in ≤_i**: Adding informational elements → decreases \(p_T+p_F\) (dilutes truth fraction). This is decoherence or phase accumulation.
- **Downward in ≤_i**: Removing informational elements → increases \(p_T+p_F\) (purifies truth fraction). This is measurement or error correction.

The Frobenius identity μ∘δ = id ensures that any round-trip through the split/fuse cycle returns the state to its original information content. The arbitrary-complex states are precisely the states that can be created by the FSPLIT of a larger state and then not fully recombined by the FFUSE — they are the "phase residues" of incomplete fusion.

### D.4 Complex Born Rule

For an arbitrary-complex state ψ with truth content \(T(\psi) = \psi \cap \{T,F\}\) and informational content \(I(\psi) = \psi \cap \{t,f\}\):

$$p_T(\psi) = \frac{|T(\psi) \cap \{T\}|}{|T(\psi)| + |I(\psi)|}$$
$$p_F(\psi) = \frac{|T(\psi) \cap \{F\}|}{|T(\psi)| + |I(\psi)|}$$

The complex structure emerges because the informational content \(|I(\psi)|\) acts as a denominator that is shared by both probabilities, exactly like the normalization factor in a complex amplitude vector. The phase information is the ratio \(|I(\psi)| / |T(\psi)|\).

**Conclusion:** The SIXTEEN_3 Born rule naturally produces three classes of states. The classical Born rule is recovered on the 3 arbitrary states. The 9 arbitrary-complex states carry the phase/information structure that the classical Born rule discards — they are the "complex" states of FDE, and their evolution under the information order is the FDE analogue of unitary evolution with phase.

---
*Reference:* QM_effects_via_FDE_and_tensor_filtration.md, Appendices B–C

132
